subject: Pathology
q: Which of the following hematological conditions is most classically associated with marked rouleaux formation on a peripheral blood smear?
why: IDA shows microcytic hypochromic cells and pencil cells, not rouleaux
Correct - elevated monoclonal paraprotein raises plasma viscosity and promotes RBC stacking, reflected in a raised ESR
CLL shows lymphocytosis with smudge cells, not rouleaux
Polycythemia vera shows raised hematocrit/RBC mass, not rouleaux
exp: Rouleaux formation (RBCs stacked like coins) results from elevated plasma proteins, most classically the monoclonal paraprotein of multiple myeloma; it correlates with a markedly raised ESR and is a bedside clue prompting serum protein electrophoresis.

subject: Pathology
q: Cerebriform (convoluted, brain-like) nuclei seen on peripheral smear in circulating malignant lymphocytes are characteristic of which condition?
why: CLL cells are small mature lymphocytes with smudge cells, not cerebriform nuclei
Hairy cell leukemia shows fine cytoplasmic projections, TRAP positive
ATLL shows flower cells with multilobated clover-leaf nuclei, HTLV-1 associated
Correct - Sezary syndrome is the leukemic phase of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, with cerebriform-nuclei malignant T cells
exp: Sezary syndrome is the leukemic phase of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides is the localized skin form); its circulating malignant CD4+ T cells with cerebriform nuclei distinguish it from the flower cells of ATLL or smudge cells of CLL.

subject: Pathology
q: Ribbon-like, intramembranous dense deposits seen on electron microscopy of a renal biopsy are diagnostic of which glomerular disease?
opts: Dense deposit disease (MPGN type II / C3 glomerulopathy)
why: Correct - dense, ribbon-like deposits within the GBM itself, driven by C3 nephritic factor and unchecked alternative complement activation
Membranous nephropathy shows subepithelial deposits with a spike-and-dome pattern
PSGN shows subepithelial humps
Minimal change disease shows no deposits, only podocyte foot process effacement on EM
exp: Dense deposit disease (MPGN type II, now under C3 glomerulopathy) is driven by C3 nephritic factor causing unchecked alternative complement activation; its EM hallmark is intramembranous ribbon-like dense deposits, distinguishing it from the subepithelial/subendothelial patterns of other glomerulonephritides. Classification terminology has evolved.

subject: Pathology
q: A medium-vessel necrotizing vasculitis that characteristically spares the lungs, is strongly associated with Hepatitis B antigenemia, and causes renal microaneurysms on angiography, best describes which condition?
why: GPA is a small-vessel, cANCA/PR3-associated vasculitis of the respiratory tract and kidneys
EGPA is associated with asthma, eosinophilia, and pANCA
Correct - PAN is medium-vessel, Hep B-linked in a minority, lung-sparing, with renal/mesenteric microaneurysms
Kawasaki disease is a medium-vessel vasculitis of childhood targeting the coronary arteries
exp: Polyarteritis nodosa is a systemic necrotizing vasculitis of medium-sized muscular arteries that spares the pulmonary circulation and is linked to chronic Hepatitis B infection in a significant minority; angiography classically shows a string of beads pattern from multiple microaneurysms, especially renal and mesenteric.

subject: Pathology
q: Calcium deposition occurring in histologically normal tissues (e.g., lung, gastric mucosa, kidney) as a consequence of hypercalcemia is termed which type of pathologic calcification?
why: Dystrophic calcification occurs in necrotic tissue with normal serum calcium
Correct - metastatic calcification is driven by hypercalcemia and deposits in normal tissue, especially kidney, lung, and gastric mucosa
Fat necrosis with saponification is a distinct process typically seen in acute pancreatitis
Caseous necrosis is a form of necrosis, not a calcification pattern
exp: Metastatic calcification is driven by a systemic derangement of calcium metabolism (hypercalcemia) and deposits in otherwise normal tissue where the local alkaline milieu favors precipitation - contrast this with dystrophic calcification, which occurs in dead or dying tissue despite normal serum calcium.

subject: Pathology
q: Ectopic secretion of antidiuretic hormone leading to the syndrome of inappropriate ADH (SIADH) is a classic paraneoplastic manifestation of which malignancy?
opts: Small cell (oat cell) carcinoma of the lung
Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung
why: Correct - the neuroendocrine origin of small cell lung carcinoma explains its propensity for ectopic ADH and ACTH secretion
Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung classically causes hypercalcemia via PTHrP, not SIADH
Renal cell carcinoma is associated with ectopic EPO (polycythemia) and hypercalcemia
Lung adenocarcinoma is not classically linked to SIADH
exp: Small cell lung carcinoma's neuroendocrine cell of origin explains its propensity for ectopic hormone secretion - SIADH (ADH) and Cushing syndrome (ACTH) - whereas squamous cell lung cancer's paraneoplastic hallmark is PTHrP-mediated hypercalcemia; this pairing is a frequently tested discriminator.

subject: Pathology
q: Clenched fists with overlapping index and fifth fingers, rocker-bottom feet, and a prominent occiput in a dysmorphic neonate are most characteristic of which chromosomal trisomy?
why: Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) features hypotonia and a single palmar crease, not this clenched-hand pattern
Trisomy 13 (Patau) features cleft lip/palate, holoprosencephaly, and polydactyly
Turner syndrome shows webbed neck and lymphedema and is not a trisomy
Correct - Trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome) has this classic clenched-fist, overlapping-finger, rocker-bottom-feet pattern
exp: Edwards syndrome (Trisomy 18) has a characteristic clenched-hand posture with the index finger overlapping the third and the fifth overlapping the fourth, combined with rocker-bottom feet and micrognathia; most affected infants die within the first year, commonly from cardiac defects or apnea.

subject: Pathology
q: A necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis affecting the upper respiratory tract, lungs, and kidneys, strongly associated with c-ANCA directed against proteinase-3, best describes which condition?
why: PAN is not ANCA-associated and spares the lungs
EGPA is pANCA/MPO-associated with asthma and eosinophilia, not destructive upper-airway disease
Correct - GPA shows cANCA/PR3 positivity with the sinonasal, pulmonary, and renal triad
Microscopic polyangiitis is pANCA/MPO-associated and lacks granuloma formation
exp: GPA (formerly Wegener granulomatosis) classically presents with the triad of sinonasal disease (including saddle-nose deformity), pulmonary nodules/cavitation, and rapidly progressive pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis; cANCA against proteinase-3 is present in most cases and correlates with disease activity.

subject: Pathology
q: Neutrophils showing bilobed, pince-nez or dumbbell-shaped nuclei with coarsely clumped chromatin, without any functional deficit, describe which finding?
why: Chediak-Higashi shows giant granules with recurrent infections and partial albinism, not nuclear hypolobation
Correct - Pelger-Huet anomaly is benign, with hyposegmented bilobed nuclei and normal neutrophil function
May-Hegglin shows giant platelets and Dohle-like inclusions with thrombocytopenia
Alder-Reilly shows coarse azurophilic granulation associated with mucopolysaccharidoses
exp: True Pelger-Huet anomaly is a benign inherited condition (lamin B receptor mutation) with normal neutrophil function despite the bizarre bilobed nuclear morphology; the acquired look-alike (pseudo-Pelger-Huet) in myelodysplastic syndrome signals marrow dysfunction, unlike the inherited form.

subject: Pathology
q: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma, the most common histologic subtype of renal cell carcinoma, is most strongly associated with loss of function/deletion of which gene?
why: Correct - clear cell RCC is characteristically associated with VHL gene inactivation, both sporadically and in von Hippel-Lindau syndrome
WT1 mutations underlie Wilms tumor, a pediatric renal neoplasm, not clear cell RCC
RET mutations underlie MEN2 syndromes
TP53 mutations span many cancers (Li-Fraumeni) but are not the defining lesion of clear cell RCC
exp: VHL gene loss leads to constitutive HIF-alpha activation and downstream VEGF/PDGF overexpression, explaining clear cell RCC's characteristic hypervascularity; this same pathway is the target of anti-angiogenic therapy (e.g., sunitinib) in metastatic disease.

subject: Pathology
q: Which serum tumour marker is most useful for monitoring a child's neuroblastoma?
why: Correct — NSE is the characteristic neuroendocrine marker elevated in neuroblastoma.
AFP is the marker for hepatocellular carcinoma and yolk sac tumour, not neuroblastoma.
CA-125 is used for epithelial ovarian carcinoma monitoring, irrelevant in a child with an abdominal neuroendocrine tumour.
PSA is prostate-specific and has no role in paediatric oncology.
exp: NSE is a cytoplasmic glycolytic enzyme released by neuroendocrine tumour cells and is elevated in neuroblastoma (as well as small cell lung carcinoma) — alongside urinary catecholamine metabolites (VMA/HVA), it is used for diagnosis and monitoring treatment response.

subject: Pathology
q: A newborn with macroglossia, omphalocele, hemihypertrophy and neonatal hypoglycemia is found to have a chromosome 11p15 imprinting abnormality. Which additional long-term risk must be screened for?
why: Retinoblastoma is linked to RB1 mutations (13q14), unrelated to the 11p15 imprinting defect of BWS.
Correct — BWS carries a well-recognised increased risk of Wilms tumour and hepatoblastoma, warranting surveillance.
Medullary thyroid carcinoma is associated with RET mutations in MEN2, not BWS.
ALL is not a specifically increased risk in BWS; the classic associated tumours are embryonal (Wilms, hepatoblastoma).
exp: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome is an overgrowth disorder from dysregulation of imprinted growth genes at 11p15 (including IGF2), and affected children need regular abdominal ultrasound and AFP screening through early childhood because of a significantly increased risk of Wilms tumour and hepatoblastoma.

subject: Pathology
q: Thread-like, ring- or figure-of-eight-shaped structures seen within red blood cells on a peripheral smear, thought to be remnants of the mitotic spindle, are known as what?
why: Howell-Jolly bodies are round basophilic nuclear DNA remnants seen in post-splenectomy/functional asplenia states, not ring/figure-8 shaped.
Heinz bodies are denatured haemoglobin precipitates seen with supravital staining in G6PD deficiency, not ring-shaped nuclear remnants.
Correct — Cabot rings are the thread-like ring/figure-of-8 inclusions of severe megaloblastic anaemia and lead poisoning.
Pappenheimer bodies are iron-containing granules seen in sideroblastic anaemia/post-splenectomy, structurally different from Cabot rings.
exp: Cabot rings are thin, looped or figure-of-eight nuclear remnants (mitotic spindle microtubule remnants) seen in red cells in severe megaloblastic anaemia and lead poisoning, reflecting abnormal erythropoiesis — they are distinct from the round nuclear (Howell-Jolly), denatured haemoglobin (Heinz), and iron-containing (Pappenheimer) inclusions.

subject: Pathology
q: A young boy with a history of recurrent haemarthroses is found to have an isolated prolongation of the activated partial thromboplastin time, with normal prothrombin time, normal platelet count and normal bleeding time. Which coagulation factor deficiency best explains this pattern?
why: Factor VII deficiency prolongs the PT (extrinsic pathway), not an isolated aPTT prolongation.
Factor X is in the common pathway, so its deficiency prolongs both PT and aPTT, not an isolated aPTT rise.
von Willebrand disease typically also prolongs the bleeding time/platelet function (via reduced platelet adhesion), which is normal here.
Correct — isolated aPTT prolongation with normal PT/platelets/bleeding time in a boy with haemarthroses is classic for X-linked Factor VIII deficiency.
exp: Haemophilia A (Factor VIII deficiency) is X-linked recessive and classically presents in boys with haemarthroses and deep muscle bleeds; because Factor VIII acts only in the intrinsic pathway, the aPTT is prolonged while the PT (extrinsic pathway) and platelet-dependent bleeding time remain normal.

subject: Pathology
q: A young woman with a strong family history of isolated microscopic haematuria but no renal failure, hearing loss or ocular defects undergoes renal biopsy, which shows diffuse thinning of the glomerular basement membrane on electron microscopy with no immune deposits. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Thin basement membrane disease (benign familial haematuria)
why: Correct — diffuse uniform GBM thinning without immune deposits, benign course, and family history of isolated haematuria defines thin basement membrane disease.
Alport syndrome shows basket-weave GBM splitting/thickening (not uniform thinning) and progresses to renal failure with deafness and lenticonus, absent here.
IgA nephropathy shows mesangial IgA deposits on immunofluorescence and typically presents with synpharyngitic gross haematuria, not this EM picture.
Minimal change disease presents with nephrotic-range proteinuria and normal light microscopy with foot process effacement on EM, not GBM thinning or isolated haematuria.
exp: Thin basement membrane disease is an autosomal dominant collagen IV disorder causing diffuse GBM thinning with isolated, usually benign, microscopic haematuria and an excellent long-term renal prognosis — unlike Alport syndrome it does not progress to renal failure and lacks the extrarenal features (sensorineural deafness, lenticonus).

subject: Pathology
q: Bronchoalveolar lavage in a patient with recurrent episodes of haemoptysis and iron-deficiency anaemia shows numerous macrophages laden with golden-brown, Prussian-blue-positive pigment. What do these cells indicate?
opts: Prior episodes of diffuse alveolar/pulmonary haemorrhage
Anthracotic pigment deposition from urban air pollution
why: Aspiration typically shows lipid-laden macrophages (oil red O positive), not iron-laden ones.
Correct — iron-positive siderophages are the hallmark of prior alveolar/pulmonary haemorrhage.
Anthracotic pigment is black carbon, not golden-brown and Prussian-blue positive, and does not correlate with haemoptysis/anaemia.
TB can cause haemoptysis, but the specific finding of iron-laden macrophages reflects haemorrhage, not granulomatous infection per se.
exp: Haemosiderin-laden macrophages (siderophages) arise when alveolar macrophages phagocytose and break down extravasated red blood cells after pulmonary haemorrhage; their presence on BAL/sputum (Prussian blue/Perls' stain positive) is objective evidence of a prior alveolar bleeding episode, as seen in Goodpasture syndrome, idiopathic pulmonary haemosiderosis, or severe mitral stenosis.

subject: Pathology
q: Within the cellular antioxidant defence system, superoxide dismutase converts superoxide radical to hydrogen peroxide. Which enzyme then detoxifies this hydrogen peroxide into water?
why: Cytochrome oxidase is a mitochondrial electron transport chain enzyme, not an antioxidant defence enzyme.
NADPH oxidase generates superoxide radical (as part of the respiratory burst), the opposite role of an antioxidant enzyme.
Correct — catalase converts hydrogen peroxide to water and oxygen, the step following SOD action.
Cyclooxygenase converts arachidonic acid to prostaglandins, unrelated to reactive oxygen species detoxification.
exp: Catalase (present in peroxisomes) and glutathione peroxidase together break down hydrogen peroxide generated by superoxide dismutase into water, completing the enzymatic detoxification of reactive oxygen species — a defect in this antioxidant cascade contributes to free-radical-mediated cell injury.

subject: Pathology
q: A patient with chemotherapy-induced marrow suppression and a platelet count of 35,000/microL is scheduled for an elective lumbar puncture. What is the minimum platelet count generally considered safe before proceeding, and is prophylactic transfusion indicated here?
opts: 100,000/microL is mandatory for any invasive procedure
At least 50,000/microL is recommended; transfuse platelets before the procedure
why: 10,000/microL is the threshold for spontaneous-bleeding prevention in stable patients, not for an invasive procedure like LP.
20,000/microL is still below the accepted safety threshold for lumbar puncture.
100,000/microL is reserved for neurosurgical or ophthalmic procedures, not a general invasive-procedure requirement.
Correct — at least 50,000/microL is the standard threshold before invasive procedures such as LP, and transfusion is indicated to reach it.
exp: While a much lower threshold (around 10,000/microL) suffices to prevent spontaneous bleeding in stable, non-bleeding patients, invasive procedures with a risk of bleeding into a closed space — such as lumbar puncture, major surgery, or central line insertion — generally require a platelet count of at least 50,000/microL, so this patient needs a prophylactic platelet transfusion beforehand. Exact cutoffs vary slightly by society and procedure.

subject: Pathology
q: Achondroplasia is caused by which type of genetic mutation?
why: FBN1 loss-of-function causes Marfan syndrome.
FMR1 CGG repeat expansion causes Fragile X syndrome.
22q11 microdeletion causes DiGeorge syndrome.
Correct — achondroplasia is caused by a gain-of-function mutation in FGFR3.
exp: Achondroplasia is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by a gain-of-function mutation in FGFR3, which impairs cartilage growth-plate proliferation and produces short-limb dwarfism; most cases arise from new mutations linked to advanced paternal age.

subject: Pathology
q: The skull X-ray of a child with transfusion-dependent beta-thalassemia major characteristically shows which finding?
why: Correct — ineffective erythropoiesis drives marrow expansion producing this classic finding.
Lacunar skull is seen with neural tube defects such as Chiari malformation/spina bifida, not thalassemia.
Battle's sign is mastoid bruising in basal skull fracture, a clinical not radiographic sign.
Copper-beaten skull reflects raised intracranial pressure or craniosynostosis.
exp: Ineffective erythropoiesis in beta-thalassemia major drives marked marrow expansion, producing the classic hair-on-end skull X-ray and chipmunk facies; regular transfusion with iron chelation prevents this bony overgrowth.

subject: Pathology
q: A peripheral smear in an elderly patient with back pain and renal failure shows red cells stacked like coins (rouleaux formation). This is most suggestive of which condition?
why: Iron deficiency anemia shows microcytic, hypochromic cells, not rouleaux.
Correct — rouleaux formation reflects elevated paraprotein raising plasma viscosity, classic in multiple myeloma.
Hereditary spherocytosis shows spherocytes on smear.
AML shows blasts, sometimes with Auer rods, not rouleaux.
exp: Rouleaux formation reflects elevated paraprotein raising plasma viscosity and reducing red cell surface-charge repulsion, a classic finding in multiple myeloma that also correlates with a markedly raised ESR; serum protein electrophoresis confirms the M-spike.

subject: Pathology
q: In massive transfusion protocol for severe obstetric hemorrhage, which ratio of packed red cells to fresh frozen plasma to platelets is currently favoured?
why: This ratio is not the evidence-based standard used in massive transfusion protocols.
This ratio is not the evidence-based standard used in massive transfusion protocols.
Correct — a 1:1:1 ratio approximates whole blood and reduces dilutional coagulopathy.
This ratio is not the evidence-based standard used in massive transfusion protocols.
exp: A 1:1:1 ratio of PRBC:FFP:platelets approximates whole blood and reduces dilutional coagulopathy during massive hemorrhage. The PROPPR trial found no survival difference versus 1:1:2 but faster hemostasis with 1:1:1, and it has been widely adopted. Exact ratios vary between massive transfusion protocols.

subject: Pathology
q: High-resolution CT of the chest showing a dilated bronchus with a diameter larger than its adjacent pulmonary artery, the signet ring sign, is diagnostic of which condition?
why: A TB cavity is a thick- or thin-walled cavity, not defined by comparison to an adjacent vessel.
Emphysema shows hyperinflation and bullae, not a signet ring pattern.
Pulmonary embolism is diagnosed by a filling defect on CT pulmonary angiography.
Correct — a bronchoarterial ratio greater than 1 (signet ring sign) is a hallmark of bronchiectasis.
exp: The signet ring sign - a dilated bronchus (the stone) next to a normal-caliber pulmonary artery (the ring), i.e. a bronchoarterial ratio greater than 1 - is a hallmark HRCT finding of bronchiectasis, which can follow prior infection, cystic fibrosis, ABPA, or ciliary dyskinesia.

subject: Pathology
q: Chronic cigarette smoking replaces the normal ciliated columnar epithelium of the bronchus with stratified squamous epithelium. This adaptive change is termed?
why: Correct — this reversible cell-type change in response to chronic irritation is metaplasia.
Dysplasia implies disordered growth with cellular atypia, a step beyond metaplasia toward malignancy.
Hyperplasia is an increase in the number of cells of the same type, not a change in cell type.
Anaplasia is loss of differentiation seen in malignant cells.
exp: Squamous metaplasia in the smoker's bronchial epithelium is a reversible adaptive response to chronic irritation; however, persistent stimulus can progress through dysplasia to squamous cell carcinoma, making it a marker of risk rather than a neoplastic change itself.

subject: Pathology
q: Serum CA 15-3 is most useful for monitoring treatment response and detecting recurrence in which malignancy?
why: CA-125 is the marker used for ovarian carcinoma.
Correct — CA 15-3 is used to monitor therapy response and recurrence in breast cancer.
CEA is used for colorectal carcinoma.
AFP is used for hepatocellular carcinoma.
exp: CA 15-3 is a glycoprotein tumour marker used to monitor therapy response and detect recurrence in breast cancer; it lacks the sensitivity and specificity needed for screening or initial diagnosis.

subject: Pathology
q: Image described: karyotype of an infant with clinical features of Down syndrome shows 46 chromosomes, with an extra copy of chromosome 21 material attached to chromosome 14. Compared to the more common trisomy 21 from meiotic nondisjunction, this translocation form has which key clinical implication?
opts: Significantly higher recurrence risk in future pregnancies if a parent is a balanced translocation carrier
Always occurs de novo, with zero recurrence risk
Is not associated with intellectual disability
why: Correct - carrier-parent status markedly raises recurrence risk.
Wrong - the phenotype is clinically indistinguishable from nondisjunction trisomy 21.
Wrong - about 25% of translocation cases are inherited from a carrier parent, not always de novo.
Wrong - intellectual disability is present as in standard trisomy 21.
exp: Translocation Down syndrome, about 3-4% of cases, requires parental karyotyping because a balanced Robertsonian translocation carrier parent confers a much higher recurrence risk than the sporadic nondisjunction form, which is age-related and has a low recurrence of about 1%; this distinction directly changes genetic counselling advice for future pregnancies.

subject: Pathology
q: Image described: bone marrow aspirate with Prussian blue (Perls') stain shows erythroid precursors with iron granules arranged in a ring around at least one-third of the nucleus. A patient on anti-tuberculous therapy develops this finding along with microcytic anaemia. The most likely offending drug and mechanism are:
opts: Isoniazid; interference with vitamin B6-dependent heme synthesis
why: Wrong - rifampicin is linked to hepatotoxicity and drug interactions, not sideroblastic anaemia.
Wrong - pyrazinamide is linked to hepatotoxicity and hyperuricemia.
Wrong - ethambutol is linked to optic neuritis, not sideroblastic anaemia.
Correct - isoniazid's pyridoxine antagonism is the classic cause.
exp: Ringed sideroblasts, iron-laden mitochondria encircling the nucleus seen on Perls'/Prussian blue stain, define sideroblastic anaemia; isoniazid is a recognised reversible drug-induced cause by antagonising pyridoxine, a cofactor for ALA synthase in heme synthesis - co-administering pyridoxine with isoniazid can prevent this in susceptible patients, as well as preventing peripheral neuropathy.

subject: Pathology
q: A 6-year-old with severe pneumonia and sepsis has a total leukocyte count of 55,000/microL with a marked left shift (increased band forms and metamyelocytes). To differentiate this leukemoid reaction from chronic myeloid leukaemia, the single most useful classic laboratory test is:
why: Wrong - morphology overlaps and is not by itself definitive.
Correct - the classic distinguishing test.
Wrong - hypercellularity is seen in both conditions.
Wrong - WBC counts can overlap significantly between the two.
exp: A leukemoid reaction is a reactive, benign, marked leukocytosis often above 50,000/microL with left shift mimicking CML, seen in severe infection, sepsis, or other stress states; the leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score is classically elevated in leukemoid reaction and reduced in CML, and definitive distinction today is by demonstrating the BCR-ABL1 fusion/Philadelphia chromosome, which is absent in leukemoid reaction.

subject: Pathology
q: A term neonate born to a previously sensitised Rh-negative mother develops jaundice and anaemia within the first day of life. To confirm the neonate's red cells are coated with maternal anti-D antibody, which test is performed on the infant's blood?
why: Wrong - indirect Coombs detects free antibody in serum, not antibody already bound to cells.
Correct - detects antibody already coating the infant's own cells.
Wrong - Kleihauer-Betke quantifies fetal cells in maternal circulation, unrelated here.
Wrong - cross-matching is done before transfusion, not to diagnose the underlying haemolysis.
exp: The direct Coombs test is positive in haemolytic disease of the newborn because the infant's own RBCs are already coated in vivo with maternal IgG anti-D that crossed the placenta; this contrasts with the indirect Coombs test, used antenatally to screen maternal serum for such antibodies before they have bound to any red cells.

subject: Pathology
q: Image described: gross lung specimen from an autopsy shows a lobe that is firm, dry, granular on cut section, and grey-tan in colour, with fibrin strands visible, occurring on day 4-6 of untreated pneumococcal pneumonia. This appearance corresponds to which stage of lobar pneumonia?
why: Wrong - congestion shows a heavy, boggy, red lung, not firm/grey.
Wrong - red hepatisation is firm and red/liver-like, not grey.
Correct - matches the firm, dry, grey-tan, granular description.
Wrong - resolution shows progressive softening as exudate is digested.
exp: Classical lobar pneumonia progresses through four stages: congestion, with vascular engorgement, to red hepatisation, RBCs plus fibrin plus neutrophils giving a liver-like red firm lung, to grey hepatisation, RBC breakdown with persistent fibrinosuppurative exudate giving a grey firm lung, to resolution, macrophage-mediated enzymatic digestion and clearing - antibiotic therapy has made the full untreated natural history uncommon to see today.

subject: Pathology
q: A patient with acute pancreatitis has serum calcium trending downward over several days. Imaging and autopsy studies in fatal cases show chalky-white deposits in the peripancreatic and omental fat. The mechanism producing both the fat necrosis and the associated hypocalcaemia is:
opts: Enzymatic (lipase-mediated) fat necrosis with saponification consuming calcium
why: Correct - describes the enzymatic saponification mechanism.
Wrong - coagulative necrosis is the pattern in most solid-organ ischaemic injury, not enzymatic fat destruction.
Wrong - liquefactive necrosis is typical of bacterial abscesses or brain infarcts.
Wrong - fibrinoid necrosis affects vessel walls in immune-mediated vasculitis/malignant hypertension.
exp: Fat necrosis in acute pancreatitis is enzymatic, not traumatic, in origin: released lipase and phospholipase A2 hydrolyse triglycerides in peri-pancreatic fat into free fatty acids, and the fatty acids chelate calcium to form soaps, seen grossly as chalky-white foci - sufficiently extensive saponification can significantly contribute to the hypocalcaemia of severe pancreatitis, itself a poor prognostic Ranson marker.

subject: Pathology
q: A surgical pathology report on a resected colonic adenocarcinoma describes the tumour as moderately differentiated and separately assigns it pT3N1M0. These two pieces of information respectively represent:
opts: Grading (differentiation) and Staging (TNM extent of spread) respectively
why: Wrong - moderately differentiated is a grading term, not staging.
Wrong - TNM is not a grading system.
Wrong - definitions reversed.
Correct - matches the true definitions of grade and stage.
exp: Grade and stage answer different questions and both must be reported: grade describes cellular differentiation/aggressiveness under the microscope, while TNM stage describes anatomic extent of disease, tumour depth, nodal spread, distant metastasis - in most cancers, stage is the stronger independent predictor of prognosis and drives treatment decisions, though grade adds prognostic refinement within a stage.

subject: Pathology
q: An Rh-negative mother delivers an Rh-positive baby. Before deciding whether the standard dose of anti-D immunoglobulin is sufficient to prevent maternal sensitisation, or whether an additional dose is needed, which test is performed to quantify the volume of fetal blood that has entered the maternal circulation?
why: Wrong - direct Coombs checks for antibody on the infant's cells, unrelated here.
Wrong - indirect Coombs screens maternal serum for free antibody, not fetal cell quantification.
Correct - quantifies fetomaternal haemorrhage to guide anti-D dosing.
Wrong - osmotic fragility is used for hereditary spherocytosis.
exp: The standard postpartum anti-D dose covers only a limited volume of fetal whole blood entering maternal circulation; the Kleihauer-Betke acid-elution test identifies fetal haemoglobin-containing RBCs, which resist acid elution, among maternal cells on a peripheral smear, allowing calculation of fetomaternal haemorrhage volume and any additional anti-D dose needed after large haemorrhages such as abruption or trauma.

subject: Pathology
q: A 62-year-old man presents with facial plethora, pruritus after a hot bath, splenomegaly, and a haemoglobin of 19 g/dL with a low serum erythropoietin level. Bone marrow shows panmyelosis. The molecular mutation most strongly associated with this condition is:
why: Wrong - BCR-ABL1 is the hallmark of CML.
Wrong - FLT3-ITD is associated with a subset of AML.
Wrong - PIGA mutation underlies paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria.
Correct - the hallmark mutation of polycythaemia vera.
exp: Polycythaemia vera is a myeloproliferative neoplasm driven in over 95% of cases by the JAK2 V617F mutation, causing constitutive JAK-STAT signalling and autonomous erythroid proliferation independent of erythropoietin - clinically reflected by a low/suppressed serum EPO level, a key clue distinguishing PV from secondary polycythaemia, where EPO is high, or relative polycythaemia.

subject: Pathology
q: A peripheral smear from a child with severe recurrent bacterial infections shows giant, abnormal lysosomal granules within neutrophils and other leukocytes. Which disorder is this most characteristic of?
why: CGD shows a negative NBT/DHR test from NADPH oxidase defect, not giant granules on smear
LAD shows markedly elevated neutrophil counts with delayed umbilical cord separation, not giant granules
Correct - giant lysosomal granules define Chediak-Higashi
MPO deficiency is usually asymptomatic and not associated with abnormal granule morphology
exp: Chediak-Higashi syndrome is caused by a LYST gene defect affecting lysosomal trafficking, producing giant dysfunctional granules along with partial albinism and recurrent pyogenic infections.

subject: Pathology
q: Which renal biopsy finding is most specific for diabetic nephropathy on light microscopy?
opts: Linear IgG deposition along the GBM
why: Diffuse mesangial expansion is the earliest and commonest finding but is not specific to diabetes alone
Correct - nodular glomerulosclerosis is pathognomonic of advanced diabetic nephropathy
Crescents suggest a rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, not diabetic nephropathy
Linear IgG deposition is the hallmark of anti-GBM disease, not diabetes
exp: Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules are eosinophilic, PAS-positive nodular masses of mesangial matrix that are pathognomonic (though not the earliest finding) of diabetic nephropathy.

subject: Pathology
q: A worker with long-standing occupational asbestos fibre exposure develops progressive exertional dyspnea. Chest X-ray shows bibasilar, lower-zone pulmonary fibrosis with bilateral pleural plaques. This disease carries a distinctive dual cancer risk - bronchogenic carcinoma synergistic with smoking, and mesothelioma independent of smoking. Which occupational lung disease is this?
why: Byssinosis is a reversible airway disease from cotton dust, no fibrosis or malignancy risk
Simple CWP shows small nodular opacities in the upper/mid zones, not lower-zone fibrosis with pleural plaques
Correct - asbestosis with lower-zone fibrosis, pleural plaques, and the dual bronchogenic carcinoma/mesothelioma risk
Silicosis causes upper-zone nodular fibrosis and does raise bronchogenic carcinoma risk, but not mesothelioma - a good distractor since it's real but wrong for the mesothelioma link
exp: Asbestosis produces bibasilar/lower-zone interstitial fibrosis with bilateral pleural plaques, and asbestos exposure carries a dual malignancy risk: bronchogenic carcinoma risk multiplies synergistically with cigarette smoking, while mesothelioma risk is independent of smoking status - a pairing not shared by silica, which raises bronchogenic carcinoma risk (IARC group 1) but not mesothelioma.

subject: Pathology
q: In a massively transfused trauma patient, which coagulation abnormality develops earliest due to dilution and consumption, mandating early empirical correction?
why: Protein C deficiency is not the primary concern in acute dilutional coagulopathy
Factor VIII is an acute-phase reactant and tends to remain relatively preserved early
Correct - fibrinogen falls earliest and is targeted first in massive transfusion protocols
Antithrombin III depletion is not the first-targeted abnormality in trauma resuscitation
exp: Fibrinogen is the first coagulation factor to fall to critically low levels during massive haemorrhage, which is why modern massive transfusion protocols give cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate early.

subject: Pathology
q: Elevated serum beta-2 microglobulin is most useful as a prognostic marker in which malignancy?
why: MTC is monitored with calcitonin and CEA
HCC is monitored with AFP, not beta-2 microglobulin
Correct - beta-2 microglobulin is part of the myeloma ISS staging
Ewing sarcoma has no established role for this marker
exp: Serum beta-2 microglobulin correlates with tumour burden and renal function in multiple myeloma and is a core component of the International Staging System.

subject: Pathology
q: A child with intellectual disability, a characteristic cat-like high-pitched cry in infancy, microcephaly, and hypertelorism is found to have a deletion on the short arm of chromosome 5. What is this condition called?
why: Angelman is a 15q11-13 maternal deletion/UBE3A defect with happy puppet phenotype
Wolf-Hirschhorn is a 4p deletion with Greek warrior helmet facies, not this cry
Correct - 5p deletion with cat-cry, microcephaly
Williams syndrome is a 7q11.23 microdeletion with elfin facies and supravalvular aortic stenosis
exp: Cri-du-chat syndrome results from a 5p deletion and classically presents with a distinctive high-pitched cat-like cry from laryngeal abnormalities, plus microcephaly, hypertelorism, and intellectual disability.

subject: Pathology
q: Peripheral smear in a patient with chronic liver disease shows red cells with multiple irregular spiky projections of varying length. What are these cells called and what is their mechanism?
opts: Echinocytes (burr cells), from renal failure alone
Acanthocytes, from altered membrane lipid composition
Target cells, from excess membrane surface area
why: Schistocytes are fragmented cells from microangiopathic hemolysis, a different morphology
Echinocytes have regular, evenly spaced projections and a different clinical association (uremia/artifact)
Correct - acanthocytes with irregular spicules in liver disease
Target cells show a central density with a surrounding pale ring, not spiky projections
exp: Acanthocytes (spur cells) arise in severe liver disease because of an abnormal cholesterol:phospholipid ratio in the red cell membrane, producing irregularly spaced, variable-length spicules.

subject: Pathology
q: A patient develops fever, hypotension, and rigors within minutes of starting a platelet transfusion; the unit was stored at room temperature. What is the most likely cause?
opts: Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction from ABO mismatch
Bacterial contamination of the platelet unit
Febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reaction from anti-HLA antibodies
why: ABO-mismatch hemolysis is more typically linked to red cell transfusion and shows hemoglobinuria/back pain
Correct - platelet storage conditions favour bacterial contamination as the cause of severe reactions
Febrile non-hemolytic reactions are usually milder, without marked hypotension
TRALI presents predominantly with acute respiratory distress/hypoxia, not primarily hypotension with rigors
exp: Platelets are stored at room temperature with agitation, which supports bacterial growth far more than refrigerated red cells; septic transfusion reaction should be suspected with high fever, rigors, and hypotension.

subject: Pathology
q: Which enzyme catalyzes conversion of the superoxide free radical (O2-) to hydrogen peroxide during oxidative cell injury?
why: Correct: SOD converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide and oxygen
Catalase acts downstream, decomposing hydrogen peroxide to water and oxygen
Glutathione peroxidase also detoxifies hydrogen peroxide and lipid peroxides using glutathione, not the initial superoxide step
Myeloperoxidase converts hydrogen peroxide and chloride to hypochlorite in neutrophil phagolysosomes, unrelated to dismutation
exp: Superoxide dismutase converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide and oxygen; catalase and glutathione peroxidase then detoxify hydrogen peroxide downstream, forming the core antioxidant defense cascade against free-radical-mediated cell injury.

subject: Pathology
q: A tumour marker used for diagnosis and post-operative surveillance of medullary carcinoma of thyroid is:
why: Thyroglobulin follows differentiated papillary or follicular carcinoma, not medullary carcinoma
Correct: calcitonin is secreted by parafollicular C cells and is the specific marker for medullary carcinoma
TSH receptor antibody is used in Graves' disease, not thyroid malignancy
PTH is a parathyroid marker, unrelated to thyroid C-cell tumours
exp: Medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from parafollicular C cells; serum calcitonin is the specific marker for diagnosis and surveillance, with CEA as a secondary marker, and is associated with MEN 2A/2B and RET mutations.

subject: Pathology
q: A tall, infertile adult male has small firm testes, gynecomastia, and elevated FSH/LH with low testosterone; karyotype is most likely:
why: 46,XY is the normal male karyotype, does not explain this phenotype
45,X is Turner syndrome, a female phenotype
Correct: 47,XXY is Klinefelter syndrome, the commonest cause of male hypogonadism/infertility
47,XYY is usually tall with normal fertility and normal testosterone
exp: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) is the commonest cause of male hypogonadism and infertility, with tall stature, small firm testes from seminiferous tubule dysgenesis, gynecomastia, and elevated gonadotropins from meiotic nondisjunction.

subject: Pathology
q: Irradiation of blood components before transfusion is primarily done to prevent which complication in immunocompromised recipients?
why: Febrile non-hemolytic reactions are prevented by leukoreduction, not irradiation
TRALI is caused by donor anti-leukocyte antibodies, unrelated to irradiation
Alloimmunization prevention relies on leukoreduction and antigen matching, not irradiation
Correct: irradiation inactivates donor T-lymphocytes, preventing TA-GVHD in severely immunocompromised recipients
exp: Gamma or X-irradiation of cellular blood products inactivates donor T-lymphocytes, preventing transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease in severely immunocompromised recipients such as those with congenital immunodeficiency, HSCT, or needing intrauterine transfusion.

subject: Pathology
q: A negative nitroblue tetrazolium (NBT) test result is diagnostic of which primary immunodeficiency?
why: Correct: defective NADPH oxidase in CGD abolishes the respiratory burst, keeping the NBT test negative
Chediak-Higashi is diagnosed by giant cytoplasmic granules on peripheral smear, NBT test is normal
LAD is diagnosed by CD18 flow cytometry, NBT test is normal
MPO deficiency usually has a normal or only mildly abnormal NBT test since NADPH oxidase is intact
exp: Chronic granulomatous disease results from defective NADPH oxidase in phagocytes, so they cannot mount a respiratory burst; the NBT test stays negative, and patients suffer recurrent infections with catalase-positive organisms like Staph aureus and Aspergillus.

subject: Pathology
q: The defining 24-hour urinary protein threshold used to diagnose nephrotic syndrome in an adult is:
why: Greater than 150mg/day is simply the upper limit of normal proteinuria
Correct: nephrotic syndrome is defined by proteinuria exceeding 3.5g/24h in adults
Greater than 1g/day is significant but subnephrotic range
Greater than 500mg/day is also subnephrotic range
exp: Nephrotic syndrome is defined by massive proteinuria exceeding 3.5 g per 24 hours in adults, along with hypoalbuminemia, generalized edema, and hyperlipidemia, distinguishing it from nephritic syndrome which features hematuria, milder proteinuria, hypertension, and RBC casts.

subject: Pathology
q: Diffuse alveolar damage with hyaline membrane formation on lung biopsy is the characteristic histology of which condition?
why: Chronic bronchitis shows Reid-index based mucous gland hyperplasia in bronchi, not alveolar hyaline membranes
Bronchiectasis shows permanent bronchial dilation with chronic inflammation, not diffuse alveolar damage
Correct: ARDS shows diffuse alveolar damage with hyaline membranes lining alveolar ducts
Sarcoidosis shows non-caseating granulomas, not hyaline membranes
exp: ARDS shows diffuse alveolar damage histologically, with hyaline membranes composed of fibrin and necrotic epithelial debris lining the alveolar ducts, resulting from increased capillary permeability in sepsis, aspiration, severe pneumonia, or trauma.

subject: Pathology
q: Anti-D immunoglobulin is administered to a Rh-negative pregnant woman at which time points to prevent alloimmunization?
opts: Only if the baby is Rh-negative
At 28 weeks gestation and within 72 hours of delivery of an Rh-positive baby
why: Delivery-only dosing misses the antenatal sensitization window
First-trimester-only dosing wanes before the highest-risk third-trimester and delivery period
Anti-D is given antenatally regardless of unknown fetal Rh status; the postnatal dose specifically requires a confirmed Rh-positive baby
Correct: standard prophylaxis is at 28 weeks and again within 72 hours postpartum if the neonate is Rh-positive
exp: Standard Rh prophylaxis gives anti-D immunoglobulin at 28 weeks gestation as a routine antenatal dose, and again within 72 hours postpartum if the neonate is confirmed Rh-positive, plus after any sensitizing event such as miscarriage, amniocentesis, or trauma.

subject: Pathology
q: A germline mutation in which tumour suppressor gene underlies Li-Fraumeni syndrome, predisposing to sarcomas, breast cancer, leukemia, and brain tumours at a young age?
why: Correct: Li-Fraumeni syndrome is caused by germline TP53 mutation, predisposing to a broad spectrum of early-onset cancers
RB1 germline mutation causes hereditary retinoblastoma and osteosarcoma predisposition, not the broad Li-Fraumeni spectrum
APC mutation causes familial adenomatous polyposis with colorectal cancer risk
BRCA1 germline mutation predisposes specifically to breast and ovarian cancer
exp: Li-Fraumeni syndrome is caused by germline TP53 mutation, the guardian of the genome, giving a markedly increased lifetime risk of multiple early-onset cancers including sarcoma, breast carcinoma, leukemia, adrenocortical carcinoma, and brain tumours, screened using the Chompret criteria.

subject: Pathology
q: Myotonic dystrophy type 1, with progressive muscle weakness, myotonia, cataracts, and cardiac conduction defects, is caused by expansion of which trinucleotide repeat?
why: CAG repeat expansion causes Huntington disease in the HTT gene, not myotonic dystrophy
Correct: CTG repeat expansion in the DMPK gene causes myotonic dystrophy type 1
CGG repeat expansion causes Fragile X syndrome in the FMR1 gene
GAA repeat expansion causes Friedreich ataxia in the FXN gene
exp: Myotonic dystrophy type 1 results from CTG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the DMPK gene on chromosome 19, showing anticipation with increasing severity and earlier onset in successive generations, like other trinucleotide repeat disorders.

subject: Pathology
q: Elongated, cigar/pencil-shaped red cells on peripheral smear are most characteristically associated with which anemia?
why: Megaloblastic anemia shows macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils, not pencil cells
Hemolytic anemia shows spherocytes or schistocytes depending on cause, not classically pencil cells
Correct: iron deficiency anemia shows microcytic hypochromic cells with elongated pencil cells or elliptocytes
Sideroblastic anemia shows a dimorphic population with ringed sideroblasts on bone marrow iron stain, not pencil cells specifically
exp: Iron deficiency anemia classically shows microcytic hypochromic red cells with marked anisopoikilocytosis, including elongated pencil cells or elliptocytes, alongside low serum ferritin and low MCV, a useful morphological clue on peripheral smear.

subject: Pathology
q: Inheritance of both copies of a chromosome from a single parent, with no contribution from the other parent, is termed?
why: Imprinting is parent-of-origin-specific gene silencing, a separate concept from UPD
Anticipation is worsening severity/earlier onset across generations, seen in trinucleotide repeat disorders
This is the correct definition of uniparental disomy
Mosaicism is the presence of two genetically distinct cell lines from a single zygote, unrelated to parental origin
exp: Uniparental disomy (UPD) occurs when both homologs of a chromosome pair come from one parent (via trisomy/monosomy rescue); it becomes clinically important when the chromosome carries imprinted genes, e.g. maternal UPD 15 causing Prader-Willi-like features.

subject: Pathology
q: Fragmented red cells (schistocytes/helmet cells) on peripheral smear accompanied by thrombocytopenia are characteristic of which group of disorders?
why: Hereditary spherocytosis shows spherocytes and a positive osmotic fragility test, not schistocytes
Schistocytes with thrombocytopenia correctly define MAHA (TTP/HUS/DIC)
G6PD deficiency shows bite cells and Heinz bodies during oxidative hemolysis
PNH shows normocytic hemolysis with a flow-cytometry CD55/CD59 deficiency, not schistocytosis
exp: Schistocytes form when RBCs are mechanically sheared crossing fibrin strands in small-vessel microthrombi - the hallmark of TTP, HUS, and DIC - and this smear finding should trigger urgent evaluation for these emergencies.

subject: Pathology
q: Co-expression of CD5 and CD23 on a monoclonal B-cell population is characteristic of which chronic lymphoproliferative disorder?
opts: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia / small lymphocytic lymphoma
why: This is the correct CD5+CD23+ immunophenotype of CLL/SLL
Mantle cell lymphoma is CD5+ but CD23-negative, with cyclin D1 overexpression
Hairy cell leukemia is TRAP-positive and CD11c/CD103+, not CD5+
Follicular lymphoma is CD10+ with t(14;18)/BCL2, not CD5+
exp: CLL/SLL is defined immunophenotypically by CD5+ CD23+ B cells (CD5 is otherwise a T-cell marker aberrantly expressed) - this distinguishes it from mantle cell lymphoma, which is CD5+ but CD23-negative and carries t(11;14)/cyclin D1.

subject: Pathology
q: Platelet concentrates for transfusion are stored under which temperature and handling condition to preserve function?
why: This is the storage condition for packed RBCs, which would rapidly impair platelet function
Freezing destroys platelet membranes without cryoprotectant
Static storage without agitation causes platelet clumping and loss of function
This is the correct standard platelet storage condition
exp: Unlike packed red cells (stored at 1-6C), platelets must be stored at room temperature (20-24C) with continuous gentle agitation to maintain viability and prevent aggregation, which also limits their shelf life to about 5 days due to bacterial contamination risk.

subject: Pathology
q: Laminated, concentrically calcified structures (psammoma bodies) may be seen histologically in which asbestos-related pleural malignancy?
why: Bronchogenic carcinoma shows keratin pearls (squamous) or glandular patterns, not psammoma bodies typically
Silicosis shows eggshell calcification of hilar nodes, not psammoma bodies
This is the correct answer - psammoma bodies occur in papillary mesothelioma
Asbestosis shows asbestos/ferruginous bodies in lung parenchyma, a different structure from psammoma bodies
exp: Psammoma bodies can be found in the papillary variant of malignant mesothelioma (also seen in papillary thyroid and serous ovarian carcinoma) - distinct from the golden-brown beaded ferruginous/asbestos bodies seen in the lung parenchyma of asbestosis.

subject: Pathology
q: Accumulation of triglyceride within hepatocyte cytoplasm as clear vacuoles is a classic example of which type of reversible cell injury?
why: Coagulative necrosis is an irreversible pattern of cell death, not a reversible change
Fatty change is correctly the prototypical reversible injury of hepatocytes
Apoptosis is programmed cell death, not an accumulation phenomenon
Dystrophic calcification occurs in dead/dying tissue with normal serum calcium, unrelated to steatosis
exp: Fatty change (steatosis) reflects reversible metabolic derangement - impaired lipoprotein export or excess substrate delivery, classically from alcohol, obesity, or toxins - and resolves with removal of the underlying cause, unlike irreversible injury patterns.

subject: Pathology
q: Bilateral ovarian metastases containing mucin-filled signet-ring cells, most often arising from a gastric primary, are termed?
why: This is the correct definition of Krukenberg tumor
Meigs syndrome is ovarian fibroma with ascites and pleural effusion, unrelated to metastasis
Struma ovarii is a monodermal teratoma composed of thyroid tissue
Brenner tumor is a benign transitional-cell epithelial ovarian tumor, not a metastasis
exp: Krukenberg tumor denotes bilateral ovarian metastases (classically from gastric signet-ring adenocarcinoma, also colon/breast) - always look for a GI primary when bilateral solid ovarian masses with signet-ring histology are reported.

subject: Pathology
q: Which blood group is considered the universal donor for packed red blood cell transfusion?
why: AB positive is the universal plasma recipient, not RBC donor
O positive still carries the Rh(D) antigen, unsafe for Rh-negative recipients
AB negative carries A and B antigens, unsafe for non-AB recipients
O negative correctly lacks all major RBC antigens
exp: O-negative red cells lack A, B, and Rh(D) antigens, so they can be transfused to any recipient in an emergency without triggering ABO/Rh-mediated hemolytic reactions - the mirror concept to AB-positive being the universal plasma recipient and AB the universal plasma donor.

subject: Pathology
q: Binucleate owl-eye cells positive for CD15 and CD30 are the neoplastic cells characteristic of:
why: DLBCL is a diffuse large B-cell proliferation without classic RS morphology or this CD15/CD30 profile
Correct - RS cells with this immunophenotype define classical Hodgkin lymphoma
Burkitt shows a starry sky pattern of monomorphic cells with a high mitotic/apoptotic rate, not RS cells
Myeloma is a plasma cell neoplasm, morphologically and immunophenotypically distinct
exp: The Reed-Sternberg cell - a giant binucleate or multinucleate cell with prominent eosinophilic owl-eye nucleoli, CD15+/CD30+ but typically CD45(LCA)-negative - is the diagnostic hallmark of classical Hodgkin lymphoma; the tumour cells are actually a minority in a reactive background of lymphocytes, eosinophils, and histiocytes.

subject: Pathology
q: Muddy brown granular casts on urine microscopy in a patient with an acute rise in serum creatinine following an episode of severe hypotension are most typical of:
why: Pre-renal azotaemia has a bland sediment with hyaline casts, since the tubules themselves are intact
AIN classically shows white cell casts and eosinophiluria, not muddy brown casts
Correct - this is the textbook cast of ATN
RPGN shows red cell casts and dysmorphic RBCs from glomerular crescents, a different lesion site
exp: Muddy brown granular casts are formed from sloughed, necrotic tubular epithelial cells and are the classic urinary sediment finding in ischaemic (or nephrotoxic) acute tubular necrosis - they distinguish intrinsic renal AKI from a purely pre-renal state, where sediment is typically bland.

subject: Pathology
q: A long-standing smoker's lung specimen shows destruction predominantly of the respiratory bronchioles in the upper lobes, with relative sparing of distal alveoli. This pattern of emphysema is:
why: Panacinar involves the whole acinus uniformly and is classic for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, lower zones
Paraseptal spares the proximal acinus and affects the distal alveolar ducts/sacs, associated with spontaneous pneumothorax in young thin men
Irregular emphysema is scar-related and has no zonal predilection
Correct - centriacinar/smoking pattern as described
exp: Smoking-related emphysema is centriacinar, upper-lobe-predominant, and starts at the respiratory bronchiole while sparing the distal acinus - this is the mirror image of alpha-1 antitrypsin-deficiency emphysema, which is panacinar and lower-lobe-predominant.

subject: Pathology
q: Within 2 hours of a plasma transfusion, a patient develops acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure with bilateral pulmonary infiltrates, but normal jugular venous pressure and no improvement with diuretics. The most likely diagnosis is:
why: Correct - non-cardiogenic pattern with normal JVP and no diuretic response fits TRALI
TACO is cardiogenic overload with raised JVP, S3, and diuretic responsiveness - the opposite picture here
Acute haemolytic reaction presents with fever, flank pain, haemoglobinuria, and DIC, not isolated respiratory failure
Anaphylaxis presents with urticaria, bronchospasm, and hypotension, typically from anti-IgA antibodies in IgA-deficient recipients
exp: TRALI is non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema caused by donor anti-leukocyte (anti-HLA/anti-HNA) antibodies triggering neutrophil-mediated capillary leak in the recipient's lungs - normal JVP and no diuretic response are the key bedside discriminators from TACO, which is cardiogenic volume overload.

subject: Pathology
q: Bilateral retinoblastoma in infants typically results from inheritance of one mutated RB1 allele, followed by somatic mutation of the second allele. This two-step mechanism of tumour-suppressor gene inactivation is described by:
why: Loss of imprinting is a distinct epigenetic mechanism (e.g., Beckwith-Wiedemann), not the RB1 two-hit model
Correct - this is Knudson's model exactly
Field cancerisation describes multiple independent premalignant clones across an exposed epithelial field (e.g., aerodigestive tract), unrelated to RB1
Loss of contact inhibition is a general property of transformed cells in culture, not a genetic mechanism
exp: Knudson's two-hit hypothesis explains why hereditary tumour-suppressor-gene cancers (retinoblastoma, familial Wilms tumour) present earlier and more often bilaterally - the first hit is already inherited in every cell, so only one somatic hit is needed to unmask the phenotype, versus two somatic hits required in sporadic cases.

subject: Pathology
q: Deletion of the maternally inherited chromosome 15q11-13 region causes Angelman syndrome (ataxia, seizures, inappropriate laughter), whereas deletion of the same region on the paternal chromosome causes Prader-Willi syndrome. This parent-of-origin-dependent gene expression is called:
why: Anticipation is worsening severity/earlier onset across generations in trinucleotide-repeat disorders (e.g., Huntington), unrelated
Mosaicism means two genetically distinct cell lines in one individual, a different phenomenon
Correct - parent-of-origin allele silencing is imprinting

Uniparental disomy (inheriting both copies of a chromosome from one parent) can also cause these syndromes without a deletion, but it is a distinct mechanism from the general term the question asks for
exp: Genomic imprinting silences one parental allele epigenetically (via methylation), so losing the still-active allele - maternal for UBE3A (Angelman) or paternal for the PWS-critical genes - produces disease even though the deleted region is identical; this pair is the classic imprinting teaching example in NEET PG genetics.

subject: Pathology
q: Peripheral smear of a patient with sickle cell disease shows nuclear remnants within RBCs staining dark purple on Wright-Giemsa stain. Their presence indicates:
opts: Megaloblastic maturation arrest in the bone marrow
why: Iron deficiency classically shows microcytic, hypochromic cells with pencil cells, not nuclear remnants
Megaloblastic change shows macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils, not Howell-Jolly bodies specifically (though they can coexist)
Lead poisoning shows coarse basophilic stippling, a ribosomal RNA finding, not a nuclear remnant
Correct - Howell-Jolly bodies signal asplenia
exp: Howell-Jolly bodies are nuclear DNA remnants normally pitted out of RBCs by a functioning spleen - their presence signals hyposplenism, which in a sickle cell patient reflects autosplenectomy from recurrent splenic infarction and predicts increased risk of encapsulated-organism sepsis (pneumococcal prophylaxis indicated).

subject: Pathology
q: Cryoprecipitate, prepared by thawing fresh frozen plasma at 1-6 degrees C, is rich in all of the following EXCEPT:
why: Correct (the exception) - factor IX is not concentrated in cryoprecipitate
Fibrinogen is a core cryoprecipitate component
Factor VIII is a core cryoprecipitate component
vWF is a core cryoprecipitate component
exp: Cryoprecipitate concentrates the cold-insoluble plasma proteins - fibrinogen, factor VIII, von Willebrand factor, factor XIII, and fibronectin - making it useful for hypofibrinogenaemia and as an adjunct in vWD/haemophilia A when specific concentrates aren't available; factor IX stays in the cryo-poor supernatant and is instead found in FFP or prothrombin complex concentrate.

subject: Pathology
q: Renal papillary necrosis is classically associated with all of the following EXCEPT:
why: Analgesic nephropathy is a classic cause of papillary necrosis
Correct (the exception) - MCD is a podocytopathy with no papillary involvement
Diabetic microangiopathy is a classic cause
Sickling in the hypoxic, hypertonic medulla is a classic cause
exp: Papillary necrosis follows medullary ischaemia and is remembered by the mnemonic POSTCARDS (Pyelonephritis, Obstruction, Sickle cell, TB, Cirrhosis, Analgesics, Renal vein thrombosis, Diabetes, Systemic vasculitis) - minimal change disease affects the glomerular podocyte, not the renal papilla, and is not a recognised cause.

subject: Pathology
q: Staging of a malignant tumor (e.g., the TNM system) is based primarily on which parameter?
why: Correct - TNM measures anatomical extent (size/invasion, nodal spread, distant metastasis) and is the strongest single prognostic predictor in most solid cancers.
Differentiation describes grade, not stage.
Mitotic rate contributes to grading, not staging.
Nuclear pleomorphism is a grading criterion, not staging.
exp: TNM staging measures anatomical extent of disease and is the strongest single predictor of prognosis in most solid tumors; grading (differentiation, mitotic rate, pleomorphism) is a separate assessment of tumor aggressiveness - don't confuse the two on the exam.

subject: Pathology
q: Deletion of the paternally-derived chromosome 15q11-13 region typically causes which imprinting disorder?
why: Angelman results from loss of the maternal allele of this region, not the paternal one.
Correct - loss of the paternal 15q11-13 allele causes Prader-Willi syndrome.
Beckwith-Wiedemann relates to 11p15 imprinting, a different locus.
Silver-Russell also involves growth/imprinting genes but a different locus.
exp: Genomic imprinting means only one parental allele is normally active. Loss of the paternal 15q11-13 allele (deletion or maternal uniparental disomy) causes Prader-Willi syndrome (hypotonia, hyperphagia, hypogonadism); loss of the same maternal allele causes Angelman syndrome - a classic paired exam fact.

subject: Pathology
q: Heinz bodies and bite cells on peripheral smear are most characteristic of which condition?
why: Spherocytosis shows spherocytes with loss of central pallor, not Heinz bodies.
Thalassemia shows target cells and microcytosis.
Correct - oxidant stress in G6PD deficiency denatures hemoglobin into Heinz bodies, which splenic macrophages pluck out, leaving bite cells.
Sideroblastic anemia shows ringed sideroblasts on bone marrow iron stain.
exp: G6PD deficiency impairs the hexose monophosphate shunt's ability to regenerate NADPH/glutathione, so oxidant triggers (infection, fava beans, dapsone, primaquine, sulfonamides) precipitate hemoglobin as Heinz bodies and drive acute hemolysis with bite cells on smear.

subject: Pathology
q: Absence of platelet membrane glycoprotein Ib, causing giant platelets and mucocutaneous bleeding, defines which inherited disorder?
why: Glanzmann involves GpIIb/IIIa, not GpIb, and platelets are normal-sized.
Chediak-Higashi is a lysosomal trafficking defect with giant leukocyte granules, not a platelet receptor defect.
Wiskott-Aldrich causes small platelets with eczema and immunodeficiency.
Correct - Bernard-Soulier is a GpIb-IX-V (vWF receptor) defect causing giant platelets and mucocutaneous bleeding.
exp: Bernard-Soulier syndrome (GpIb-IX-V defect, giant platelets) and Glanzmann thrombasthenia (GpIIb/IIIa defect, normal platelet size) are the two classic inherited platelet receptor disorders to distinguish on the exam - remember which receptor and which platelet size goes with each.

subject: Pathology
q: Diffuse thickening of the glomerular basement membrane with subepithelial 'spike and dome' deposits on silver stain is characteristic of which nephropathy?
why: Correct - subepithelial immune complex deposits (often anti-PLA2R-mediated) grow spikes of basement membrane matrix around them, giving the 'spike and dome' silver-stain appearance.
Minimal change disease shows no deposits on light/EM apart from podocyte foot process effacement.
FSGS shows segmental sclerosis, not spike-and-dome deposits.
MPGN shows a 'tram-track' double-contour basement membrane.
exp: Membranous nephropathy is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in non-diabetic adults; its subepithelial deposits produce the 'spike and dome' pattern on silver stain, distinct from the tram-tracking of MPGN.

subject: Pathology
q: Spiral mucus plugs and eosinophil-derived hexagonal crystals in the sputum of an asthmatic are called, respectively:
why: Ferruginous/asbestos bodies are seen in asbestosis lung tissue, not asthma sputum.
Correct - Curschmann spirals are mucus casts of small airways and Charcot-Leyden crystals are crystallized eosinophil granule protein.
Psammoma bodies occur in papillary thyroid/ovarian tumors, Reinke crystals in Leydig cells.
Mallory bodies occur in alcoholic liver disease, Councilman bodies in viral hepatitis.
exp: Curschmann spirals and Charcot-Leyden crystals are classic, though non-specific, sputum findings of eosinophilic airway inflammation in bronchial asthma - a favourite pathology one-liner.

subject: Pathology
q: Liquefactive necrosis, with digestion of dead tissue into a viscous liquid mass, is most typical of which process?
why: MI causes coagulative necrosis, preserving architecture initially.
Renal infarcts are also coagulative (wedge-shaped, pale).
Correct - the brain's high lipid content and lack of collagen support let hydrolytic enzymes and microglia digest infarcted tissue into a liquid mass with cystic cavitation.
Splenic infarcts are also coagulative.
exp: Cerebral infarction is the classic exception to coagulative necrosis seen in most solid-organ ischemia, undergoing liquefactive necrosis instead because the brain lacks the structural collagen framework that preserves tissue outline elsewhere.

subject: Pathology
q: Which ABO blood group is the 'universal plasma donor', safe to transfuse to a recipient of unknown blood group?
why: O plasma contains both anti-A and anti-B antibodies, unsafe for non-O recipients.
A plasma has anti-B antibody.
B plasma has anti-A antibody.
Correct - AB plasma has neither anti-A nor anti-B antibody, so it can be given to any ABO group.
exp: Group AB is the universal plasma donor (no anti-A/anti-B antibodies) while group O is the universal red cell donor (no A/B antigen) - the two rules run in opposite directions and are commonly flipped by mistake.

subject: Pathology
q: A disease that becomes more severe and presents at an earlier age in successive generations, due to expansion of a CAG trinucleotide repeat, best describes which phenomenon and disease?
why: Correct - anticipation is worsening severity/earlier onset across generations from progressive trinucleotide repeat expansion, classically Huntington disease (CAG repeat).
Imprinting explains parent-of-origin-dependent expression, not generational worsening.
Mosaicism describes two cell lines within one individual, unrelated to this phenomenon.
Uniparental disomy is inheriting both copies of a chromosome from one parent, a different mechanism.
exp: Anticipation (Huntington disease, myotonic dystrophy, fragile X) results from unstable trinucleotide repeats that expand further with each generation of gametogenesis - keep it distinct from imprinting, which is about which parental allele is silenced, not repeat expansion.

subject: Pathology
q: Spur cells (acanthocytes) with irregular thorny projections on peripheral smear are classically seen in which condition?
why: IDA shows microcytic hypochromic cells and pencil cells, not acanthocytes.
Correct - altered plasma lipoprotein composition in severe liver disease raises membrane cholesterol relative to phospholipid, distorting red cells into spiny acanthocytes.
Megaloblastic anemia shows macro-ovalocytes.
Spherocytosis shows small round cells lacking central pallor.
exp: Acanthocytes (spur cells, irregular spicules) in severe liver disease should be distinguished from echinocytes (burr cells, regular short spicules) seen in uremia - a frequently confused smear-morphology pair.

subject: Pathology
q: Blue-grey cytoplasmic inclusions in neutrophils (Dohle bodies), seen along with toxic granulation, indicate which process?
why: CML shows a spectrum of maturing myeloid cells with basophilia and low LAP score, not Dohle bodies.
Megaloblastic anemia causes hypersegmented neutrophils, not Dohle bodies.
Correct - Dohle bodies are residual rough ER seen during accelerated 'toxic' granulopoiesis in severe bacterial infection/sepsis.
Chediak-Higashi shows giant lysosomal granules, a distinct inherited defect.
exp: Dohle bodies plus toxic granulation and cytoplasmic vacuolation are bedside smear clues to a reactive (infective) leukocytosis rather than a neoplastic one - useful when a JMO is deciding whether a raised WBC needs urgent haematology referral.

subject: Pathology
q: A young boy has hematuria, bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, and anterior lenticonus. Electron microscopy of a renal biopsy shows irregular thickening, thinning, and lamellated splitting of the glomerular basement membrane in a basket-weave pattern. Diagnosis?
why: Thin basement membrane disease shows a uniformly thin, not split basket-weave, GBM with usually isolated benign hematuria.
Membranous nephropathy shows subepithelial deposits with a spike and dome pattern, not basket-weave splitting.
Fabry disease shows lamellated lipid zebra bodies in podocytes, not GBM splitting.
Correct — basket-weave GBM plus deafness and lenticonus is classic Alport syndrome.
exp: Alport syndrome results from mutated type IV collagen (commonly COL4A5, X-linked), producing an irregularly thickened, split, basket-weave GBM on EM. The triad of hematuria, sensorineural deafness, and ocular lenticonus (anterior bulging of the lens) is the classic clinical clue tying the imaging finding to the diagnosis.

subject: Pathology
q: A 40-year-old with longstanding asthma and peripheral eosinophilia develops new mononeuritis multiplex and palpable purpura. Biopsy shows necrotizing vasculitis with eosinophilic infiltration and extravascular granulomas. Which antibody is most characteristically associated?
why: Correct — MPO-ANCA (p-ANCA) is the typical serologic association in eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
c-ANCA/PR3 is characteristic of granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener's), which lacks the asthma-eosinophilia phenotype.
Anti-GBM antibody causes Goodpasture syndrome (pulmonary hemorrhage plus glomerulonephritis), a different mechanism.
Anti-Jo-1 is associated with antisynthetase syndrome/dermatomyositis, unrelated to this vasculitis.
exp: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Churg-Strauss syndrome) affects small-to-medium vessels in patients with asthma and peripheral eosinophilia, and is most commonly p-ANCA/MPO-ANCA positive — contrast this with granulomatosis with polyangiitis, which is predominantly c-ANCA/PR3 positive and lacks the asthma history.

subject: Pathology
q: Histology of a small muscular artery shows bright eosinophilic, amorphous, proteinaceous material replacing the vessel wall with luminal narrowing. This pattern is most typically seen in which condition?
why: Coagulative necrosis preserves cell/tissue outlines in a firm, pale infarct — a parenchymal, not vascular-wall, pattern.
Correct — fibrinoid necrosis of the vessel wall is the hallmark lesion of malignant hypertension.
Caseous necrosis is granular, cheese-like necrosis within TB granulomas, not a vessel-wall lesion.
Fat necrosis shows chalky-white saponification of adipose tissue, unrelated to vessel-wall pathology.
exp: Fibrinoid necrosis is deposition of fibrin and plasma proteins within vessel walls, producing a smudgy, bright pink, amorphous appearance on H&E. It is the hallmark vascular lesion of malignant hypertension (hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis) and immune-mediated vasculitides — a pattern to distinguish clearly from parenchymal necrosis types.

subject: Pathology
q: A young girl has recurrent epistaxis and menorrhagia with a prolonged bleeding time, mildly prolonged aPTT, and a normal platelet count. Ristocetin-induced platelet aggregation is reduced. Diagnosis?
why: Hemophilia A prolongs aPTT with a normal bleeding time and no mucocutaneous bleeding pattern.
Bernard-Soulier syndrome also reduces RIPA (GP1b deficiency) but classically causes thrombocytopenia with giant platelets, not a normal count.
Glanzmann thrombasthenia (GPIIb/IIIa deficiency) has normal RIPA since platelet-platelet aggregation via fibrinogen, not vWF binding, is defective.
Correct — normal platelet count with reduced RIPA and a mixed bleeding-time/aPTT picture is classic von Willebrand disease.
exp: Von Willebrand disease is the most common inherited bleeding disorder. Deficient or dysfunctional vWF impairs platelet adhesion (prolonging bleeding time and reducing ristocetin-induced platelet aggregation) and lowers factor VIII levels (mildly prolonging aPTT), while the platelet count itself stays normal — the combination that separates it from Bernard-Soulier syndrome.

subject: Pathology
q: A boy has intellectual disability, a long face, large everted ears, and macroorchidism, with similarly affected maternal male relatives. This trinucleotide repeat disorder involves expansion in which gene?
why: HTT (CAG repeat) causes Huntington disease — adult-onset chorea and dementia, not this phenotype.
DMPK (CTG repeat) causes myotonic dystrophy — myotonia and muscle weakness, not this phenotype.
Correct — FMR1 CGG repeat expansion and silencing causes Fragile X syndrome.
FXN (GAA repeat) causes Friedreich ataxia — ataxia and cardiomyopathy, not this phenotype.
exp: Fragile X syndrome results from CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion and hypermethylation-silencing of FMR1 on the X chromosome. The classic phenotype — intellectual disability, long face, large ears, and post-pubertal macroorchidism — plus X-linked inheritance explaining affected maternal-line male relatives, is a favourite genetics one-liner.

subject: Pathology
q: A young adult has dark morning urine, hemolytic anemia, and recurrent unusual-site venous thrombosis. Flow cytometry shows deficient CD55 and CD59 on red cells. This arises from a somatic mutation in which gene?
why: Correct — PIGA mutation impairs GPI-anchor synthesis, causing loss of CD55/CD59 in PNH.
ANK1 mutations cause hereditary spherocytosis via ankyrin defects in the RBC membrane skeleton, not complement dysregulation.
G6PD deficiency causes oxidative hemolysis with Heinz bodies/bite cells, not CD55/59 loss.
ADAMTS13 deficiency/inhibition causes TTP through unregulated vWF multimers, an unrelated mechanism.
exp: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria arises from an acquired somatic PIGA mutation in a hematopoietic stem cell, impairing GPI-anchor synthesis so complement-regulatory proteins CD55 (decay-accelerating factor) and CD59 (MAC-inhibitory protein) are lost from the cell surface — causing complement-mediated hemolysis plus a hypercoagulable, thrombosis-prone state.

subject: Pathology
q: A t(14;18) translocation causing BCL2 overexpression and resistance to apoptosis is characteristic of which lymphoma?
why: Burkitt lymphoma is driven by t(8;14) with MYC overexpression, causing a highly proliferative starry sky lymphoma.
Mantle cell lymphoma is driven by t(11;14) with cyclin D1 (CCND1) overexpression.
Correct — t(14;18)/BCL2 overexpression defines follicular lymphoma.
DLBCL is genetically heterogeneous (BCL6, BCL2, MYC rearrangements across subtypes) and behaves aggressively, unlike the indolent course here.
exp: Follicular lymphoma is driven by t(14;18)(q32;q21), which juxtaposes BCL2 next to the IGH enhancer. Overexpressed BCL2 blocks apoptosis in germinal-center B cells, producing the indolent, follicular-pattern lymphoma typical of older adults — a classic genetics-to-morphology link.

subject: Pathology
q: In a stable, afebrile, non-bleeding hospitalized adult with no procedure planned, prophylactic platelet transfusion is generally indicated once the platelet count falls below which threshold?
why: 50,000/microL is closer to the threshold used before major surgery or invasive procedures, not routine prophylaxis.
30,000/microL is not a standard prophylactic cutoff in this setting.
20,000/microL may be used if additional bleeding risk factors (fever, sepsis, coagulopathy) are present, not the baseline stable-patient threshold.
Correct — 10,000/microL is the standard prophylactic trigger in stable, non-bleeding adults.
exp: Randomized trial evidence and AABB guidance (Kaufman RM et al., Ann Intern Med 2015;162(3):205-213) support a prophylactic platelet transfusion trigger of 10,000/microL in stable, afebrile, non-bleeding hospitalized patients, with higher thresholds reserved for active bleeding or before invasive procedures.

subject: Pathology
q: A heavy smoker develops ipsilateral ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis along with shoulder and arm pain, due to an apical lung tumor invading the sympathetic chain. Syndrome?
why: Correct — an apical (superior sulcus) tumor invading the sympathetic chain producing Horner's triad plus brachial plexus pain is Pancoast syndrome.
SVC syndrome causes facial/neck swelling and distended neck veins from venous obstruction, not Horner's triad.
Carcinoid syndrome causes flushing, diarrhea, and bronchospasm from vasoactive amines, unrelated to local tumor invasion.
Eaton-Lambert (myasthenic) syndrome causes proximal weakness improving with repeated use, a paraneoplastic neuromuscular disorder, not a local invasion syndrome.
exp: A superior sulcus (Pancoast) tumor at the lung apex can invade the stellate ganglion/sympathetic chain, producing Horner's syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis) together with brachial plexus involvement causing shoulder and arm pain, often with rib destruction on imaging.

subject: Pathology
q: Histology of an old area of fat necrosis shows granular basophilic calcium deposits within the necrotic debris, in a patient with normal serum calcium. This process is termed?
why: Metastatic calcification occurs in previously normal tissues and requires an elevated serum calcium/phosphate product.
Heterotopic ossification is formation of true bone in soft tissue, not amorphous calcium salt deposition.
Correct — dystrophic calcification occurs in necrotic or damaged tissue despite normal serum calcium.
Calciphylaxis is small-vessel calcification with skin necrosis, classically in end-stage renal disease with deranged calcium-phosphate metabolism.
exp: Dystrophic calcification is calcium deposition in dead or damaged tissue despite normal serum calcium levels — classically seen in old necrotic foci, atherosclerotic plaques, and damaged heart valves — distinguishing it from metastatic calcification, which requires hypercalcemia and deposits in otherwise normal tissue.

subject: Pathology
q: Cancer cells preferentially use aerobic glycolysis for energy production even when oxygen is abundant. This metabolic reprogramming is known as?
why: The Pasteur effect is the opposite phenomenon — oxygen suppressing glycolysis in normal cells.
The Bohr effect describes CO2/H+-driven rightward shift of the O2-hemoglobin dissociation curve, unrelated to cancer metabolism.
The Crabtree effect is glucose-induced suppression of oxidative respiration in yeast/some normal cells, a distinct phenomenon.
Correct — the Warburg effect is the cancer-specific shift to aerobic glycolysis.
