exp: The Warburg effect describes cancer cells' preference for glycolysis for ATP generation even in normoxia, supplying glycolytic intermediates for biosynthesis of nucleotides, lipids, and proteins needed for rapid proliferation — the metabolic hallmark exploited diagnostically by FDG-PET imaging.

subject: Pathology
q: A patient develops a falling platelet count 5-10 days after starting heparin, along with a new arterial or venous thrombosis. The causative antibodies are directed against which complex?
why: GPIIb/IIIa-fibrinogen is the complex disrupted in Glanzmann thrombasthenia, an inherited receptor deficiency, not an antibody-mediated disease.
Correct — heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is caused by IgG antibodies against platelet factor 4 bound to heparin.
GP1b-vWF interaction is defective in Bernard-Soulier syndrome, an inherited receptor deficiency.
ADAMTS13 deficiency/inhibition causes uncleaved ultra-large vWF multimers in TTP, a different mechanism from HIT.
exp: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is caused by IgG antibodies against platelet factor 4-heparin complexes; these immune complexes activate platelets via their Fc receptors, causing thrombocytopenia paradoxically accompanied by a prothrombotic, thrombosis-prone state — heparin must be stopped immediately and replaced with a non-heparin anticoagulant.

subject: Pathology
q: Fibrillin-1 (FBN1) gene mutation causing Marfan syndrome is located on which chromosome?
why: Correct - FBN1 is located at 15q21.1, encoding fibrillin-1.
Chromosome 21 is linked to Down syndrome (trisomy 21), not Marfan.
Chromosome 7 carries CFTR (cystic fibrosis), unrelated to Marfan.
Chromosome 11 carries the beta-globin gene cluster (sickle cell/thalassemia), unrelated.
exp: FBN1 on chromosome 15q21.1 encodes fibrillin-1, a major glycoprotein of extracellular microfibrils; its mutation causes autosomal dominant Marfan syndrome with aortic root dilatation, arachnodactyly, and lens dislocation as classic triad features.

subject: Pathology
q: Caseous necrosis with a cheese-like, friable gross appearance is most classically seen in which condition?
why: Correct - caseous necrosis with granulomatous inflammation is the hallmark of tuberculosis.
Acute pancreatitis shows enzymatic fat necrosis with chalky calcium soap deposits, not caseous necrosis.
Myocardial infarction shows coagulative necrosis with preserved cell outlines.
Cerebral infarct characteristically undergoes liquefactive necrosis, not caseous.
exp: Caseous necrosis combines features of coagulative and liquefactive necrosis, producing soft, friable, yellow-white debris with complete loss of tissue architecture surrounded by a granulomatous rim - the hallmark of tuberculous granulomas.

subject: Pathology
q: Atypical reactive lymphocytes with cytoplasm indented by adjacent red cells are characteristic of which condition?
why: Correct - EBV-driven infectious mononucleosis produces large atypical reactive lymphocytes with scalloped cytoplasm.
CLL shows small mature lymphocytes with smudge cells, not large atypical reactive cells.
ALL shows blasts with scant cytoplasm, often TdT positive, not atypical reactive lymphocytes.
Hairy cell leukemia shows cells with fine cytoplasmic projections and TRAP positivity.
exp: Infectious mononucleosis, caused by EBV, produces atypical (Downey) lymphocytes on peripheral smear - large reactive T cells with abundant basophilic cytoplasm scalloped by adjacent red cells - alongside lymphadenopathy, fever, and a positive heterophile (Monospot) test.

subject: Pathology
q: Which morphological feature distinguishes apoptosis from necrosis?
opts: Massive calcium influx causing cell swelling
Cell shrinkage with chromatin condensation and apoptotic body formation, without inflammation
why: This describes necrosis, not apoptosis
Karyolysis/liquefaction are necrotic changes
Calcium influx/swelling marks irreversible necrotic injury
Correct - shrinkage, chromatin condensation, apoptotic bodies, no inflammation
exp: Apoptosis is programmed cell death marked by cell shrinkage, chromatin condensation, nuclear fragmentation, and formation of membrane-bound apoptotic bodies that are phagocytosed without triggering inflammation, unlike necrosis.

subject: Pathology
q: Serum PSA (prostate-specific antigen) as a screening tool for prostate cancer has which important limitation?
opts: It is elevated only in metastatic disease
It lacks specificity, being elevated also in BPH and prostatitis
It is not produced by normal prostate tissue
It cannot be measured in blood
why: PSA can be elevated in localized disease too, not only metastatic disease
Correct - PSA is organ-specific but not cancer-specific
PSA is normally produced by both benign and malignant prostatic epithelium
PSA is measured routinely in serum - that is the basis of the test
exp: PSA is organ-specific but not cancer-specific - it is elevated in benign conditions such as BPH and prostatitis, leading to false positives and potential over-investigation.

subject: Pathology
q: Target cells on a peripheral blood smear are characteristically seen in all of the following EXCEPT:
why: Thalassemia classically shows target cells
Liver disease causes target cells from increased membrane cholesterol
Splenectomy removes the filter that normally clears target cells, so they persist/increase
Correct exception - HS shows spherocytes, not target cells
exp: Target cells (codocytes) result from an increased membrane-to-volume ratio and appear in thalassemia, liver disease, and post-splenectomy states; hereditary spherocytosis instead shows spherocytes from a decreased surface-to-volume ratio.

subject: Pathology
q: S-100 protein is an immunohistochemical marker most useful in confirming which type of tumour?
why: HCC marker is Hep Par-1/AFP
CEA is the standard colorectal marker
Correct
PSA/PSAP mark prostatic carcinoma
exp: S-100 protein, derived from neural crest tissue, is a sensitive immunohistochemical marker for malignant melanoma, and also stains schwannomas, neurofibromas, and Langerhans cells.

subject: Pathology
q: Golden-brown, iron-protein-coated fibres seen on lung histology in a shipyard worker with lower-lobe pulmonary fibrosis and pleural plaques are known as?
why: Psammoma bodies are laminated calcified structures in papillary thyroid/serous ovarian carcinoma and meningioma
Curschmann's spirals are mucous plugs seen in asthmatic sputum
Charcot-Leyden crystals are eosinophil-derived crystals also seen in asthma
Correct
exp: Ferruginous (asbestos) bodies — asbestos fibres coated with an iron-protein complex, dumbbell-shaped on H&E — are the histological hallmark of asbestosis, causing lower-lobe/subpleural fibrosis, pleural plaques, and a raised risk of bronchogenic carcinoma and mesothelioma, with smoking multiplying the lung cancer risk.

subject: Pathology
q: Giant cytoplasmic granules in neutrophils, partial oculocutaneous albinism, and recurrent pyogenic infections in a child are characteristic of which disorder?
why: Correct — the LYST-gene defect gives the giant-granule/albinism/infection triad
CGD is due to NADPH oxidase defect with catalase-positive organism infections and an abnormal DHR/NBT test, no giant granules or albinism
LAD presents with delayed umbilical cord separation and absent pus formation, no giant granules
Job/hyper-IgE syndrome shows coarse facies, eczema, and cold (non-inflamed) abscesses, not giant granules
exp: Chediak-Higashi syndrome (autosomal recessive LYST gene mutation) causes defective lysosomal trafficking, producing giant cytoplasmic granules visible in neutrophils/leukocytes on peripheral smear, partial oculocutaneous albinism, and recurrent pyogenic infections — a classic image-based triad worth recognizing on sight.

subject: Pathology
q: A sandblaster with 20 years of occupational dust exposure presents with progressive breathlessness. Chest X-ray shows numerous small nodular opacities predominantly in the upper lung zones, with eggshell calcification of the hilar lymph nodes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Asbestosis shows ferruginous bodies with lower-lobe fibrosis and pleural plaques, not eggshell hilar calcification
Correct
Coal workers' pneumoconiosis shows coal macules, upper-lobe predominant, but without eggshell calcification
Berylliosis produces non-caseating granulomas mimicking sarcoidosis, not eggshell calcification
exp: Silicosis, from chronic inhalation of crystalline silica dust (sandblasting, mining, stone-cutting), classically produces upper-lobe predominant small nodular opacities and pathognomonic eggshell calcification of hilar lymph nodes; silicotic nodules also raise the risk of TB reactivation (silicotuberculosis).

subject: Pathology
q: Which immunohistochemical marker is characteristically positive in tumors of mesenchymal origin, such as sarcomas?
why: Cytokeratin marks epithelial tumors (carcinomas), the opposite lineage
Correct — vimentin is the broad intermediate-filament marker of mesenchymal-origin cells and their tumors
Desmin is more specific, marking muscle differentiation (rhabdomyosarcoma, leiomyosarcoma) within the mesenchymal group rather than being a general marker
Chromogranin marks neuroendocrine tumors
exp: Vimentin is an intermediate filament expressed by cells of mesenchymal origin (fibroblasts, endothelium) and their tumors — sarcomas — making it a broad screening marker used alongside more specific markers (desmin for muscle, CD31/34 for vascular) to confirm mesenchymal lineage and distinguish sarcomas from carcinomas (cytokeratin-positive) and lymphomas (CD45-positive).

subject: Pathology
q: Which tumour marker is characteristically markedly elevated in choriocarcinoma and used to monitor treatment response?
why: Correct — choriocarcinoma arises from trophoblastic tissue secreting beta-hCG
AFP is elevated in yolk sac tumour and HCC, not typically in pure choriocarcinoma
CA-125 is a non-specific epithelial ovarian cancer marker
LDH is a nonspecific tumour-bulk marker, not specific like beta-hCG
exp: Choriocarcinoma arises from trophoblastic tissue, which secretes beta-hCG; serial beta-hCG titres are used both for diagnosis and to monitor treatment response/remission in gestational trophoblastic disease.

subject: Pathology
q: Antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels, causing proximal muscle weakness that paradoxically improves with repeated muscle use, are a classic paraneoplastic association of which lung cancer subtype?
why: Squamous cell carcinoma is classically linked to PTHrP-mediated hypercalcemia, not this syndrome
Adenocarcinoma is the commonest lung cancer subtype overall but has no classic link to this syndrome
Correct — small cell carcinoma is the classic malignancy associated with Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome
Large cell carcinoma shares some neuroendocrine features with small cell but is not the classic association
exp: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels, reducing acetylcholine release) is the classic paraneoplastic neuromuscular syndrome of small cell lung carcinoma; unlike myasthenia gravis, weakness improves with repeated contraction, and CMAP amplitude increases on high-frequency repetitive nerve stimulation.

subject: Pathology
q: Hypercalcemia as a paraneoplastic manifestation of squamous cell carcinoma of the lung is mediated by:
why: ACTH causes Cushing syndrome, classically small cell carcinoma
ADH causes SIADH, classically small cell carcinoma
Correct - the classic humoral hypercalcemia mechanism in squamous cell lung ca
Marrow infiltration causes local osteolytic hypercalcemia, not this paraneoplastic mechanism
exp: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung is the classic cause of humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy via ectopic secretion of PTH-related peptide (PTHrP), distinct from small cell carcinoma's SIADH/Cushing associations.

subject: Pathology
q: Terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) positivity on immunophenotyping is characteristic of:
why: Correct - TdT marks immature lymphoblasts, defining ALL/lymphoblastic lymphoma
AML is usually TdT-negative and MPO/CD13/CD33-positive instead; only a minority (M0/M1) show weak TdT
CLL is a mature B-cell neoplasm, TdT-negative
Myeloma is a mature plasma cell neoplasm, TdT-negative
exp: TdT (terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase) positivity marks immature lymphoblasts and is a key immunophenotypic discriminator of acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma from mature lymphoid neoplasms (CLL, myeloma); AML is usually TdT-negative (MPO/CD13/CD33-positive instead), though a minority - chiefly minimally differentiated AML (M0/M1) - can show weak TdT positivity.

subject: Pathology
q: Which karyotype and clinical triad best describe Turner syndrome?
opts: 45,X; webbed neck, coarctation of aorta, streak gonads
why: 47,XXY with gynecomastia describes Klinefelter syndrome, a male phenotype
Correct classic Turner karyotype and clinical triad
47,XXX (triple X syndrome) usually has a near-normal phenotype with tall stature and normal fertility, unrelated to Turner syndrome
46,XX with virilization and raised 17-OHP describes congenital adrenal hyperplasia
exp: Turner syndrome (45,X or mosaic variants) presents with short stature, webbed neck, low posterior hairline, streak gonads causing primary amenorrhoea/infertility, and strong association with coarctation of the aorta and bicuspid aortic valve — echocardiography is mandatory at diagnosis.

subject: Pathology
q: Nodular glomerulosclerosis (Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesions) on renal biopsy is the classic histological finding in which condition?
why: Correct — the eponymous lesion of diabetic nephropathy
Minimal change disease shows normal light microscopy with isolated podocyte foot process effacement, no nodules
IgA nephropathy shows mesangial IgA deposits with variable proliferation, not nodular sclerosis
PSGN shows subepithelial humps on EM, not nodular mesangial sclerosis
exp: Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules are eosinophilic, PAS-positive nodular deposits of mesangial matrix within glomeruli, representing the classic diagnostic lesion of diabetic nephropathy, typically appearing after long-standing hyperglycaemia and correlating with progressive proteinuria and declining renal function.

subject: Pathology
q: Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) is most useful as a tumour marker for monitoring recurrence in which malignancy, though it is not recommended as a screening test?
why: Hepatocellular carcinoma is monitored with alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), not CEA
Epithelial ovarian carcinoma is monitored with CA-125, not CEA
Pancreatic carcinoma is monitored with CA 19-9, not CEA
Correct — CEA is the classic colorectal carcinoma recurrence marker
exp: CEA is a glycoprotein tumour marker most classically associated with colorectal carcinoma, used post-operatively to monitor for recurrence rather than for screening or diagnosis, since it lacks the sensitivity/specificity for standalone screening and can be elevated in smokers and various benign conditions.

subject: Pathology
q: Which immunohistochemical marker is most useful in identifying neuroendocrine tumors such as carcinoid and pheochromocytoma?
why: Correct, marks neurosecretory granules in neuroendocrine cells
Desmin marks muscle/myogenic tumors
Vimentin is a nonspecific mesenchymal marker
Cytokeratin marks epithelial tumors broadly, not neuroendocrine-specific
exp: Chromogranin A (along with synaptophysin) is the standard IHC marker for neuroendocrine differentiation - carcinoid tumors, pheochromocytoma, small cell lung carcinoma, and medullary thyroid carcinoma all stain positive.

subject: Pathology
q: A neonate with microcephaly, a high-pitched cat-like cry, hypertelorism, and severe intellectual disability is found to have a deletion involving the short arm of a chromosome. Which chromosome is involved?
why: Correct, partial deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5
Williams syndrome (7q11.23) presents with elfin facies and supravalvular aortic stenosis, not a cat-cry
Prader-Willi/Angelman involve 15q11-13 imprinting defects, not this phenotype
DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2) presents with cardiac defects, hypocalcemia, and immunodeficiency, not this phenotype
exp: The distinctive high-pitched, cat-like cry in infancy (from laryngeal hypoplasia) is pathognomonic for Cri-du-chat syndrome (5p deletion) and is a favorite image/audio-description-based NEET PG discriminator among the microdeletion syndromes.

subject: Pathology
q: Concentric, laminated calcified structures called psammoma bodies are characteristically seen in which group of neoplasms?
opts: Follicular thyroid carcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma, and Wilms tumor
Papillary thyroid carcinoma, serous cystadenocarcinoma of ovary, and meningioma
Medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and carcinoid tumor
Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma, glioblastoma, and neuroblastoma
why: These tumors are not classically associated with psammoma bodies
Correct, the classic psammoma-body-bearing tumor group
Medullary thyroid carcinoma shows amyloid deposits, not psammoma bodies
Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma and glioblastoma are undifferentiated tumors not associated with this finding
exp: Psammoma bodies are dystrophic calcifications forming in areas of slow tumor necrosis and are a helpful histologic clue linking an easily-remembered group: papillary thyroid carcinoma, ovarian serous cystadenocarcinoma, meningioma, and mesothelioma.

subject: Pathology
q: Non-caseating granulomas composed of epithelioid histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells, in the absence of any identifiable infectious organism, along with elevated serum ACE levels, are characteristic of which condition?
why: TB classically produces CASEATING granulomas with demonstrable acid-fast bacilli, not non-caseating
Correct, sarcoidosis is defined by non-caseating granulomas with no identifiable infectious cause and supportive elevated ACE
GPA classically shows necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis with c-ANCA positivity
Histoplasmosis typically produces necrotizing granulomas with visible yeast forms on special stains
exp: The caseating vs non-caseating distinction is the single most important histologic discriminator between tuberculosis and sarcoidosis on biopsy - sarcoidosis granulomas lack central necrosis and stains for AFB/fungi are negative, while elevated ACE (produced by epithelioid cells within the granulomas) supports but does not confirm the diagnosis.

subject: Pathology
q: Coagulative necrosis, characteristic of ischemic infarction in most solid organs (except the brain), is explained by which mechanism that transiently preserves tissue architecture?
opts: Denaturation of structural and enzymatic proteins blocks proteolysis of the dead cells
why: Wrong — liquefactive, not coagulative, necrosis results from neutrophilic enzymatic digestion, as in the brain or an abscess.
Correct — protein/enzyme denaturation prevents autolysis, preserving the cell outline (coagulative pattern).
Wrong — caseous necrosis is a distinct pattern (TB) with a friable cheese-like center and granulomatous inflammation, no preserved architecture.
Wrong — fat necrosis with saponification is seen in acute pancreatitis, a separate pattern from coagulative necrosis.
exp: In coagulative necrosis, ischemic injury denatures both structural proteins and lysosomal/cytoplasmic enzymes, so proteolytic autolysis of the dead cell is blocked — the cell's basic outline persists for days despite the cell being dead. Seen in most solid-organ infarcts (heart, kidney, spleen) except the brain, which undergoes liquefactive necrosis due to its high lipid content and lack of a supportive stroma.

subject: Pathology
q: Ischemia-reperfusion injury paradoxically worsens tissue damage upon restoration of blood flow, primarily due to generation of which species?
opts: Increased ATP production overwhelming the cell
why: Wrong — ATP is actually depleted during ischemia; its restoration alone does not cause the injury.
Wrong — bile pigment deposition is unrelated to ischemia-reperfusion pathophysiology.
Correct — an oxidative burst generating reactive oxygen species on reoxygenation is the principal mechanism of reperfusion injury.
Wrong — complement activation does contribute, but the primary paradoxical driver is oxidative stress, not complement-independent lysis.
exp: Reperfusion injury occurs when restoring oxygen to previously ischemic tissue triggers a burst of reactive oxygen species (via reintroduced oxygen acting on incompletely reduced oxygen intermediates from damaged mitochondria, the xanthine oxidase pathway, and activated neutrophils), combined with calcium overload and complement activation — paradoxically amplifying injury beyond ischemia alone. Relevant in MI thrombolysis/PCI, stroke reperfusion, and transplant graft reperfusion.

subject: Pathology
q: A child with nephrotic syndrome has a renal biopsy showing normal glomeruli on light microscopy but diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes on electron microscopy, with no immune deposits. What is the diagnosis?
why: Wrong — membranous nephropathy shows subepithelial deposits with a spike-and-dome pattern on EM/silver stain, not an absence of deposits.
Correct — normal light microscopy, no immune deposits, and isolated foot process effacement on EM is diagnostic of MCD.
Wrong — FSGS shows segmental sclerosis in some glomeruli visible on light microscopy, not a normal picture.
Wrong — MPGN shows mesangial/endothelial proliferation and tram-track basement membrane splitting on light microscopy, not a normal picture.
exp: Minimal change disease — the commonest cause of nephrotic syndrome in children (roughly 80-90%) — shows normal glomeruli on light microscopy, negative immunofluorescence, and isolated diffuse podocyte foot process effacement visible only on EM. Responds excellently to steroids (over 90% remission); biopsy is generally reserved for steroid-resistant or atypical cases.

subject: Pathology
q: A young man develops gross hematuria 1-2 days after an upper respiratory tract infection, with mesangial IgA deposits on renal biopsy. What is the diagnosis?
why: Wrong — post-streptococcal GN has a longer latency (1-3 weeks after streptococcal infection), not 1-2 days.
Wrong — anti-GBM disease shows linear IgG deposits, not mesangial IgA, and often presents with pulmonary hemorrhage.
Correct — synpharyngitic hematuria with mesangial IgA deposits is classic IgA nephropathy.
Wrong — HSP nephritis is histologically identical but requires systemic features (purpura, arthritis, abdominal pain), absent here.
exp: IgA nephropathy (Berger disease) is the most common glomerulonephritis worldwide, characterized by classic synpharyngitic hematuria occurring within 1-3 days of a URTI (versus post-streptococcal GN's typical 1-3 week latency), with mesangial IgA deposition on immunofluorescence. HSP nephritis is histologically identical but accompanied by systemic features — a purely renal presentation favors isolated IgA nephropathy.

subject: Pathology
q: A disorder is transmitted only through affected mothers to their children, with variable severity among siblings depending on the proportion of mutant versus normal organelle genomes in each cell. Which inheritance pattern does this best describe?
why: Autosomal dominant conditions are transmitted by either parent, not exclusively maternally
X-linked recessive disorders affect sons of carrier mothers, with daughters typically unaffected carriers — not this pattern
Correct — maternal-only transmission with variable severity from heteroplasmy is the hallmark of mitochondrial inheritance
Genomic imprinting causes parent-of-origin-dependent expression of a single gene copy, not this maternal-transmission-with-heteroplasmy pattern
exp: Mitochondrial DNA is inherited almost exclusively from the ovum's cytoplasm, so mitochondrial disorders show strict maternal transmission; because a cell's mitochondria are a mixed population of mutant and normal mtDNA (heteroplasmy), the proportion inherited by each tissue or offspring varies, explaining the wide variability in disease severity.

subject: Pathology
q: Segmental sclerosis and hyalinosis involving only some glomeruli, with the remainder appearing normal on light microscopy, is characteristic of which condition?
why: Correct — focal plus segmental sclerosis/hyalinosis defines FSGS.
Wrong — minimal change disease is normal on light microscopy, diagnosis needs EM.
Wrong — membranous nephropathy shows diffuse subepithelial spike-and-dome deposits, not segmental sclerosis.
Wrong — diffuse proliferative GN shows global hypercellularity of nearly all glomeruli, as in lupus nephritis class IV.
exp: FSGS is defined by sclerosis/hyalinosis that is both focal (affecting some glomeruli) and segmental (affecting part of a glomerulus), and is the commonest cause of steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome, contrasting with minimal change disease which looks normal on light microscopy and needs EM to show podocyte foot-process effacement.

subject: Pathology
q: Which of the following events marks the point of no return (irreversibility) in hypoxic cell injury?
opts: Reversible ribosomal detachment from rough endoplasmic reticulum
Depletion of ATP with anaerobic glycolysis
Massive calcium influx with severe mitochondrial vacuolization
why: Cellular and mitochondrial swelling is an early, reversible change that resolves if the injurious stimulus is removed.
Ribosomal detachment (reducing protein synthesis) is likewise an early reversible change.
ATP depletion with a shift to anaerobic glycolysis is the initial reversible biochemical response to hypoxia.

Correct — sustained, massive calcium influx causing severe mitochondrial vacuolization (mitochondrial permeability transition) and profound membrane damage marks the transition to irreversible injury.
exp: Cell injury remains reversible through ATP depletion, anaerobic glycolysis, cellular/mitochondrial swelling, and ribosomal detachment — all correctable if the stimulus is removed. The point of no return is defined by massive, sustained calcium influx causing severe mitochondrial vacuolization (mitochondrial permeability transition pore opening) and profound plasma/lysosomal membrane damage, after which the cell cannot recover.

subject: Pathology
q: A 45-year-old man's myocardium undergoes acute severe ischemia for 20 minutes, then reperfusion is restored. Electron microscopy of the affected myocytes at this stage shows large amorphous flocculent densities within swollen mitochondria. This finding indicates:
opts: Reversible injury with cell recovery still possible
Irreversible injury with cell death now inevitable
why: Reversible injury shows mitochondrial swelling with normal-density matrix, not amorphous deposits
Coagulative necrosis is a light-microscopic/gross description that develops hours later, not this EM finding
Correct — flocculent mitochondrial densities (calcium-phosphate precipitates) are the ultrastructural marker of irreversibility
Fatty change is cytoplasmic lipid vacuolation, unrelated to mitochondrial calcium deposits
exp: Large amorphous flocculent densities in swollen mitochondria are calcium-phosphate precipitates from massive Ca2+ influx — the classic ultrastructural marker separating reversible from irreversible cell injury, appearing before light-microscopic necrosis is visible.

subject: Pathology
q: A 32-year-old non-smoker with early-onset dyspnoea and cirrhosis is found to have panacinar emphysema predominantly involving the lower lobes on CT chest. The most likely underlying cause is:
why: Correct — young non-smoker with panacinar lower-lobe emphysema plus cirrhosis is the classic A1AT-deficiency picture
Smoking-related emphysema is centriacinar and upper-lobe predominant, and occurs in smokers
Bronchiectasis shows dilated thick-walled bronchi on imaging, not panacinar emphysema, and doesn't explain the liver disease
Hypersensitivity pneumonitis causes granulomatous interstitial disease, not emphysema, and has no link to cirrhosis
exp: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes unopposed neutrophil elastase activity, producing panacinar, lower-lobe-predominant emphysema at a young age, often in non-smokers, alongside hepatic cirrhosis from misfolded Z-allele protein accumulating in hepatocytes — early emphysema plus liver disease should always trigger A1AT-level testing.

subject: Pathology
q: Bundles of Auer rods within the cytoplasm of abnormal promyelocytes, described as faggot cells, are characteristic of which condition?
opts: Chronic myeloid leukemia in blast crisis
why: AML M2 may show single Auer rods but not the characteristic bundled faggot pattern
Correct — faggot cells with t(15;17) PML-RARA define acute promyelocytic leukemia/M3
CML blast crisis is a different leukemia altogether, not defined by faggot cells
ALL is lymphoblastic — Auer rods are a myeloid marker and are not seen in ALL
exp: Faggot cells - abnormal promyelocytes packed with numerous Auer rod bundles - are the classic morphological clue to acute promyelocytic leukemia (AML M3), driven by the t(15;17) PML-RARA fusion. Recognizing this on a smear matters clinically because APML carries a high risk of DIC and responds to ATRA-based therapy, distinct from other AML subtypes.

subject: Pathology
q: A 45-year-old man presents with marked leukocytosis (WBC 1,80,000/uL) showing a full spectrum of granulocyte maturation on peripheral smear (myelocytes through mature neutrophils), splenomegaly, and a low leukocyte alkaline phosphatase (LAP) score. Which cytogenetic abnormality is most characteristic of this condition?
why: t(15;17) PML-RARA is diagnostic of acute promyelocytic leukaemia (AML M3)
t(14;18) BCL2-IGH is characteristic of follicular lymphoma
t(11;14) CCND1-IGH (cyclin D1) is characteristic of mantle cell lymphoma
Correct
exp: Chronic myeloid leukaemia is defined by the t(9;22)(q34;q11) reciprocal translocation forming the Philadelphia chromosome and the BCR-ABL1 fusion gene, which produces a constitutively active tyrosine kinase — the target of imatinib and other TKIs. The clinical picture (marked leukocytosis with a full maturation spectrum, splenomegaly, low LAP score) is classic CML.

subject: Pathology
q: Honeycombing with subpleural and basal predominant fibrosis on lung biopsy is characteristic of which interstitial lung disease?
why: Correct — subpleural/basal honeycombing defines UIP
NSIP shows uniform, temporally homogeneous fibrosis, typically without honeycombing
Hypersensitivity pneumonitis shows bronchiolocentric granulomas with upper/mid-zone predominance
Sarcoidosis shows non-caseating granulomas along lymphatic routes, not honeycombing
exp: Usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP), the pathological correlate of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, shows temporally and spatially heterogeneous fibrosis with subpleural/basal honeycombing and fibroblastic foci — the key discriminator from NSIP, which is temporally uniform and lacks honeycombing.

subject: Pathology
q: Central caseation necrosis surrounded by epithelioid cells, Langhans giant cells, and a lymphocytic cuff on histopathology is characteristic of which of the following?
why: Sarcoid granulomas are classically non-caseating (naked epithelioid granulomas without central necrosis) - the opposite of this description.
Foreign body giant cell granulomas form around inert material, lack caseation, and giant cells have haphazardly scattered nuclei, not the peripheral horseshoe arrangement of Langhans cells.
Correct - the classic caseating granuloma of tuberculosis.
Rheumatoid nodules show central fibrinoid necrosis with palisading histiocytes, not true caseation or Langhans giant cells.
exp: Caseating (soft, cheese-like) central necrosis surrounded by epithelioid histiocytes, Langhans-type multinucleated giant cells, and a peripheral lymphocytic rim is the histological hallmark of tuberculous granuloma - the single most important granuloma pattern to recognise on NEET PG pathology slides.

subject: Pathology
q: Small cell carcinoma of the lung is classically associated with ectopic secretion of which hormone, leading to hyponatremia?
why: Correct - ectopic ADH from small cell carcinoma causes SIADH and hyponatraemia.
PTHrP-driven hypercalcaemia is the classic paraneoplastic syndrome of squamous cell lung carcinoma, not small cell.
Ectopic ACTH also occurs in small cell carcinoma but causes Cushing syndrome (hypokalaemic alkalosis), not the hyponatraemia asked about here.
Calcitonin excess is associated with medullary thyroid carcinoma, not lung cancer.
exp: Small cell (oat cell) lung carcinoma is the classic cause of paraneoplastic SIADH from ectopic ADH secretion by neuroendocrine tumour cells, producing dilutional hyponatraemia - one of several small cell paraneoplastic syndromes (alongside ectopic ACTH/Cushing and Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome), and a favourite discriminator against squamous cell carcinoma's PTHrP-mediated hypercalcaemia.

subject: Pathology
q: Numerous smudge (basket) cells on peripheral smear are characteristically seen in which condition?
why: AML shows blasts with Auer rods, not smudge cells
Hairy cell leukemia shows cells with fine hairy cytoplasmic projections and is TRAP-positive
Correct - smudge cells are classic for CLL
Infectious mononucleosis shows atypical reactive (Downey) lymphocytes, not smudge cells
exp: Smudge (basket) cells - fragile neoplastic small lymphocytes that rupture during smear preparation - are a hallmark peripheral blood finding in chronic lymphocytic leukemia, reflecting membrane fragility of the clonal B lymphocytes.

subject: Pathology
q: A neonate with a conotruncal cardiac defect, hypocalcemia, and thymic hypoplasia is found to have a 22q11.2 microdeletion. Which syndrome does this represent?
why: Williams syndrome is due to a 7q11.23 microdeletion, presenting with elfin facies, supravalvular aortic stenosis, and hypercalcemia - not this triad.
Prader-Willi syndrome results from loss of paternal 15q11-q13 genes, presenting with neonatal hypotonia and later hyperphagia, not cardiac, thymic, or parathyroid defects.
Correct - 22q11.2 microdeletion (DiGeorge syndrome) causes CATCH-22 features: Cardiac defects, Abnormal facies, Thymic hypoplasia, Cleft palate, Hypocalcemia.
Cri-du-chat syndrome is due to a 5p deletion, presenting with a characteristic cat-like cry and microcephaly, not this combination.
exp: 22q11.2 microdeletion syndrome (DiGeorge syndrome) classically presents with the CATCH-22 features: Cardiac defects (conotruncal, e.g. tetralogy of Fallot, truncus arteriosus), Abnormal facies, Thymic hypoplasia/aplasia (T-cell immunodeficiency), Cleft palate, and Hypocalcemia (parathyroid hypoplasia). Confirm with FISH or microarray for the 22q11.2 deletion.

subject: Pathology
q: Image described: peripheral smear from a microcytic anaemic child shows coarse basophilic stippling in red cells, with normal iron studies. This finding should shift the diagnosis away from beta-thalassemia trait toward:
why: Iron deficiency anaemia shows pencil cells and anisopoikilocytosis, not basophilic stippling
Hereditary spherocytosis shows spherocytes with increased osmotic fragility, unrelated to stippling
Anaemia of chronic disease shows normocytic/mildly microcytic cells with low TIBC, not stippling
Correct - coarse basophilic stippling is the classic discriminator pointing to lead poisoning over thalassemia trait
exp: Coarse basophilic stippling reflects lead-induced inhibition of pyrimidine 5'-nucleotidase (impaired RNA degradation in reticulocytes) and is classic for lead poisoning; beta-thalassemia trait typically shows microcytosis with target cells but WITHOUT prominent basophilic stippling, making this smear finding the key discriminator that should prompt a blood lead level and an exposure history.

subject: Pathology
q: Which tumor marker is most useful for monitoring treatment response and detecting recurrence in carcinoma of the pancreas?
why: AFP is the marker for hepatocellular carcinoma and yolk sac tumors, not pancreatic cancer
Beta-hCG is used for choriocarcinoma and other germ cell tumors
Correct — CA 19-9 is the standard marker for pancreatic adenocarcinoma follow-up
CEA is primarily a colorectal cancer marker, less sensitive and specific for pancreatic cancer than CA 19-9
exp: CA 19-9, a sialylated Lewis antigen, is the tumor marker of choice for pancreatic adenocarcinoma — used for monitoring treatment response and detecting recurrence. It is falsely low or absent in Lewis-antigen-negative individuals (about 5-10% of the population) and can be falsely elevated in obstructive jaundice from any cause, so it is not used for screening.

subject: Pathology
q: Leukocyte alkaline phosphatase (LAP) score is characteristically low in which condition?
why: Leukemoid reaction shows a high LAP score, the opposite pattern
Pregnancy is a physiological state associated with a raised LAP score
Correct — CML is the classic condition with a low LAP score
Infective or reactive neutrophilia raises the LAP score
exp: LAP score discriminates CML (low, due to the neoplastic granulocyte clone) from a leukemoid reaction (high) — both can present with markedly raised WBC counts and left shift, so this stain is the classic bedside differentiator.

subject: Pathology
q: Which tumour marker is most useful for monitoring epithelial ovarian carcinoma?
why: AFP marks yolk sac tumours and hepatocellular carcinoma, not epithelial ovarian cancer.
CEA is the standard marker for colorectal and pancreatic cancer; it is not the primary ovarian marker.
hCG marks germ cell tumours (choriocarcinoma) and gestational trophoblastic disease.
Correct - CA-125 is elevated in most epithelial ovarian carcinomas and tracks treatment response and recurrence.
exp: CA-125 is the standard tumour marker for monitoring epithelial (serous) ovarian carcinoma treatment response and detecting recurrence, though it lacks specificity for screening as it also rises in endometriosis, PID, pregnancy, and menstruation.

subject: Pathology
q: What is the earliest reversible ultrastructural change in a cell following hypoxic injury?
why: Karyolysis (nuclear dissolution) is a late, irreversible marker of cell death, not an early reversible change.
Coagulative necrosis is the irreversible tissue-level outcome of infarction, occurring hours after the initial insult.
Dystrophic calcification develops in already-necrotic tissue over a longer time course, not as an early ultrastructural event.
Correct - ATP depletion impairs the Na+-K+ ATPase pump, causing intracellular sodium and water influx and producing cellular and mitochondrial swelling.
exp: The earliest reversible morphological response to hypoxic/ischemic cell injury is cellular and mitochondrial swelling, from ATP depletion, Na+-K+ ATPase pump failure, and consequent Na+/water influx. If the insult persists, injury becomes irreversible - marked by severe mitochondrial vacuolization, plasma membrane damage, and nuclear changes (pyknosis to karyorrhexis to karyolysis).

subject: Pathology
q: Subepithelial hump-shaped deposits on electron microscopy of a renal biopsy are characteristic of which glomerular disease?
why: Anti-GBM disease shows linear IgG deposition along the GBM, not discrete humps.
IgA nephropathy shows mesangial IgA deposits, typically with synpharyngitic hematuria.
Correct — subepithelial humps define post-streptococcal/post-infectious GN.
Lupus nephritis class IV shows subendothelial wire-loop deposits, a different location.
exp: Pattern recognition on renal biopsy: subepithelial humps = post-streptococcal GN; subendothelial wire loops = lupus nephritis class IV; linear IgG along GBM = anti-GBM/Goodpasture disease; mesangial IgA = IgA nephropathy. Post-streptococcal GN classically follows a latent period of 1-3 weeks after pharyngitis or 3-6 weeks after skin infection, presenting with cola-colored urine, oliguria, and hypertension in a child.

subject: Pathology
q: Hypersegmented neutrophils (nuclei with 5 or more lobes) on a peripheral blood smear are most characteristic of which type of anemia?
why: Correct
Iron deficiency anemia shows microcytic hypochromic cells with anisopoikilocytosis (pencil cells), not hypersegmented neutrophils
Hemolytic anemia shows polychromasia, spherocytes/schistocytes and reticulocytosis depending on cause, not hypersegmentation
Aplastic anemia shows pancytopenia with a hypocellular marrow, without this specific neutrophil morphology
exp: Hypersegmented neutrophils (nuclear lobe count 5-6 or more) are a classic peripheral smear finding in megaloblastic anemia (B12 or folate deficiency), reflecting impaired DNA synthesis that affects myeloid precursors as well as erythroid ones. This finding, along with oval macrocytes, often predates the fall in hemoglobin and is a useful early diagnostic clue.

subject: Pathology
q: Which tumor marker is most useful for hepatocellular carcinoma and endodermal sinus (yolk sac) tumor?
why: CA-125 tracks epithelial ovarian carcinoma, not HCC.
Correct — AFP is produced by hepatocellular carcinoma and yolk-sac tumor cells.
CA 19-9 is the standard marker for pancreatic and colorectal carcinoma.
PSA is prostate-specific and irrelevant to liver or germ-cell tumors.
exp: AFP is the classic tumor marker for hepatocellular carcinoma and yolk sac (endodermal sinus) tumor, and is also used in antenatal screening (elevated in neural tube defects, reduced in Down syndrome).

subject: Pathology
q: A 6-year-old with beta-thalassaemia major, transfused irregularly only when haemoglobin falls to 6-7 g/dL, has frontal bossing and maxillary overgrowth. Image described: lateral skull radiograph showing widening of the diploic space with perpendicular trabecular spicules, a hair-on-end appearance. What is the pathological basis?
opts: Osteoclastic resorption driven by secondary hyperparathyroidism
Subperiosteal new bone formation due to vitamin C deficiency
Massive expansion of erythroid marrow with thinning of the overlying cortex
why: Secondary hyperparathyroidism causes generalised resorption and brown tumours, not radial diploic spicules
Scurvy gives subperiosteal haemorrhage and new bone, with a very different clinical picture
Correct: chronic anaemia drives erythropoietin, erythroid hyperplasia expands the medullary cavity and thins the cortex, producing hair-on-end skull and chipmunk facies
Osteoblastic metastases are sclerotic deposits, not seen in a 6-year-old with thalassaemia
exp: Untreated chronic anaemia drives erythropoietin, and erythroid marrow hyperplasia expands the medullary cavity: hair-on-end skull, chipmunk or rodent facies, thinned cortex with pathological fracture, and paraspinal extramedullary haematopoietic masses. This is exactly why we hypertransfuse to keep pre-transfusion haemoglobin at 9-10.5 g/dL - it suppresses the marrow and prevents all of it. The same appearance occurs in sickle cell disease.

subject: Pathology
q: In a fetus with deletion of all four alpha-globin genes presenting as hydrops fetalis, which abnormal haemoglobin predominates?
why: HbH is the beta4 tetramer of three-gene deletion (HbH disease), which survives to present as haemolytic anaemia
Correct: with no alpha chains at all, gamma chains form gamma4 tetramers - Hb Bart - giving hydrops fetalis incompatible with extrauterine life
HbS requires a beta-globin point mutation and normal alpha chains
HbA2 is a normal minor adult haemoglobin and requires alpha chains
exp: Learn the alpha-thalassaemia genotype ladder: one gene deleted is a silent carrier; two is alpha-thal trait (microcytosis with a NORMAL HbA2, which is why it hides on HPLC); three is HbH disease (beta4 tetramers, haemolytic anaemia); four is Hb Bart (gamma4) hydrops fetalis. Both Hb Bart and HbH have very high oxygen affinity and deliver almost no oxygen to tissues.

subject: Pathology
q: An 18-year-old with transfusion-dependent thalassaemia on irregular chelation (ferritin 4200 ng/mL) presents with dyspnoea, oedema and an irregular pulse. Echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 34%. Which statement about this complication is correct?
opts: Cardiac iron overload is the leading cause of death in transfusion-dependent thalassaemia
Hepatocellular carcinoma is the commonest cause of death in this population
Serum ferritin correlates precisely with myocardial iron, making cardiac T2-star MRI unnecessary
Cardiac iron deposition is irreversible and chelation offers no benefit once ejection fraction falls
why: Correct: transfusional haemosiderosis loads the heart, and iron cardiomyopathy with heart failure or arrhythmia remains the commonest cause of death
Hepatic iron and hepatitis C do raise hepatocellular carcinoma risk, but cardiac disease still leads mortality
Ferritin correlates only loosely with myocardial iron, which is precisely why cardiac T2-star MRI is the standard (below 20 ms means loading, below 10 ms high risk)
Iron cardiomyopathy is substantially reversible with intensified chelation, deferiprone being the most effective for cardiac iron
exp: Cardiac iron overload is the leading cause of death in transfusion-dependent thalassaemia. Serum ferritin tracks myocardial iron only loosely, so cardiac T2-star MRI guides therapy: below 20 ms indicates loading and below 10 ms is high risk. The damage is substantially reversible with intensified chelation, and deferiprone is the best chelator for cardiac iron. The commonest endocrine complication overall is hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.

subject: Pathology
q: Sydenham chorea is thought to result from antibodies raised against which group A streptococcal antigen, cross-reacting with neuronal antigens in the basal ganglia?
why: Correct: M protein epitopes mimic basal ganglia neuronal antigens (and cardiac myosin in carditis).
Wrong: streptolysin O is a haemolysin, not implicated in neuronal cross-reactivity.
Wrong: the hyaluronic acid capsule is identical to host hyaluronate and is non-immunogenic.
Wrong: C5a peptidase degrades a complement chemotaxin; it is not linked to chorea.
exp: M protein epitopes structurally mimic neuronal antigens in the caudate and subthalamic nuclei - molecular mimicry, a type II hypersensitivity mechanism. The same M-protein mimicry against cardiac myosin and valve glycoproteins produces rheumatic carditis, which is why one antigen explains two very different organ manifestations.

subject: Pathology
q: A pathologic lead point found at laparotomy in an 8-year-old with ileocecal intussusception shows sheets of monomorphic lymphoid cells with a 'starry sky' pattern on histology. Which underlying diagnosis and genetic hallmark best fit this picture?
opts: Burkitt lymphoma; t(8;14) translocation involving c-myc
why: Wrong: Reed-Sternberg cells define Hodgkin lymphoma, not a monomorphic starry-sky picture.
Correct: starry-sky pattern plus t(8;14) MYC-IGH is Burkitt lymphoma, the classic ileocaecal lead point in older children.
Wrong: neuroblastoma shows small round blue cells with Homer-Wright rosettes, not a starry-sky lymphoid pattern.
Wrong: Wilms tumour is a renal tumour with triphasic histology, unrelated to bowel lead points.
exp: Burkitt lymphoma shows a 'starry sky' pattern - sheets of high-grade lymphoblasts studded with tingible-body macrophages clearing apoptotic debris - and characteristically carries the t(8;14) translocation, which places the c-myc oncogene under the immunoglobulin heavy-chain enhancer, driving relentless proliferation. It is the lymphoma most associated with ileocecal intussusception as a pathologic lead point in older children.

subject: Pathology
q: Increased osmotic fragility of red blood cells in hypotonic saline, due to a reduced RBC surface-area-to-volume ratio, is characteristic of which condition?
exp: Hereditary spherocytosis results from membrane cytoskeletal protein defects (spectrin, ankyrin, band 3) that make RBCs spherical instead of biconcave, lowering their surface-area-to-volume ratio and making them lyse earlier in hypotonic saline -- the basis of the osmotic fragility test. Thalassemia and iron deficiency, by contrast, produce microcytic cells with decreased osmotic fragility because their flattened shape gives excess membrane relative to volume.

subject: Pathology
q: Which statement best characterises autosomal recessive primary microcephaly (MCPH)?
opts: Normal intelligence in nearly all affected individuals despite the small head
Congenital, non-progressive microcephaly with variable intellectual disability, and increased risk in consanguineous unions
X-linked inheritance with disease expression only in males
Onset after 2 years of age with entirely normal development until then
why: Wrong: most people with MCPH have mild-to-moderate intellectual disability.
Correct: MCPH is congenital, non-progressive, autosomal recessive, with variable ID and higher risk with consanguinity.
Wrong: MCPH is autosomal recessive, not X-linked.
Wrong: in MCPH the small head is present at birth; late onset fits acquired or progressive causes such as Rett syndrome.
exp: MCPH is a genetically heterogeneous group of autosomal recessive disorders (MCPH1, ASPM and others) causing microcephaly that is present at birth and does not progress, with variable intellectual disability. Contrast with progressive postnatal microcephaly (Rett syndrome, metabolic and degenerative disease), where the head circumference is normal at birth and falls away later.

subject: Pathology
q: A cytochemical stain positive for which enzyme characteristically supports a diagnosis of hairy cell leukemia?
exp: Hairy cell leukemia, an indolent B-cell neoplasm typically of older adults, shows TRAP-positive cytoplasmic granules on cytochemistry and fine hair-like cytoplasmic projections on peripheral smear. Patients classically present with pancytopenia and massive splenomegaly, and bone marrow aspiration often yields a 'dry tap' from marrow fibrosis.

subject: Pathology
q: Auer rods in leukemic blast cells are most characteristic of which condition?
exp: Auer rods are needle-shaped, peroxidase-positive cytoplasmic inclusions formed from fused azurophilic granules, seen in myeloblasts of acute myeloid leukemia; bundles of them are classic for acute promyelocytic leukemia (AML M3). They are absent in ALL, which may instead show PAS-positive blocks in lymphoblasts.

subject: Pathology
q: Eggshell calcification of hilar lymph nodes on chest X-ray is characteristically seen in which occupational lung disease?
why: Asbestosis causes pleural plaques and lower-lobe fibrosis
Correct: eggshell calcification of hilar nodes is classic for silicosis
Coal workers' pneumoconiosis can rarely show it, but it is far less characteristic than in silicosis
Byssinosis is reversible airway disease from cotton dust, with no nodal calcification
exp: Eggshell (rim) calcification of hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes is a characteristic radiological finding in silicosis, seen in workers exposed to crystalline silica dust (mining, sandblasting, stone-cutting), and silicosis also increases susceptibility to tuberculosis (silicotuberculosis).

subject: Pathology
q: On renal biopsy immunofluorescence, linear deposition of IgG along the glomerular basement membrane is characteristic of which condition?
why: Post-streptococcal GN shows granular lumpy-bumpy deposits
Membranous nephropathy shows granular subepithelial spike-and-dome deposits
IgA nephropathy shows mesangial IgA deposits
Correct: linear IgG along the GBM is anti-GBM (Goodpasture) disease, against the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen
exp: Linear IgG (often with C3) deposition along the glomerular basement membrane on immunofluorescence is pathognomonic of anti-GBM (Goodpasture) disease, reflecting antibodies against the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen. This contrasts with the granular subepithelial humps of post-streptococcal GN, the granular subepithelial spike-and-dome deposits of membranous nephropathy, and the mesangial IgA deposits of IgA nephropathy.

subject: Pathology
q: Wire-loop capillary lesions on renal biopsy light microscopy are classically seen in which condition?
why: Minimal change disease looks normal on light microscopy; only foot-process effacement on EM
Membranous nephropathy shows diffuse GBM thickening with spikes on silver stain, not wire loops
Correct: wire loops reflect massive subendothelial immune deposits, the hallmark of class IV lupus nephritis
FSGS shows segmental sclerosis and hyalinosis, not wire-loop thickening
exp: Wire-loop lesions result from massive subendothelial immune complex deposition and are the classic light-microscopy hallmark of diffuse proliferative lupus nephritis (WHO/ISN-RPS Class IV), the most severe and common renal biopsy pattern in SLE, warranting aggressive immunosuppression.

subject: Pathology
q: A binucleate cell with prominent eosinophilic nucleoli giving an owl-eye appearance is characteristic of:
why: Burkitt lymphoma shows a starry-sky pattern of uniform medium-sized cells
Myeloma shows sheets of plasma cells with eccentric clock-face nuclei
Correct: the owl-eye Reed-Sternberg cell (CD15+, CD30+) is the hallmark of classical Hodgkin lymphoma
CML shows leucocytosis with the full myeloid series and basophilia
exp: The Reed-Sternberg cell is the hallmark of Hodgkin lymphoma and is CD15 and CD30 positive. It is not by itself pathognomonic - similar cells occur in infectious mononucleosis - so the surrounding reactive infiltrate matters for the diagnosis.

subject: Pathology
q: Positive cytoplasmic myeloperoxidase (MPO) staining in leukemic blasts is most useful for confirming which diagnosis?
why: Correct — MPO is specific to the granulocytic (myeloid) lineage, confirming a myeloid blast population.
ALL blasts are MPO-negative and are instead marked by TdT and lymphoid antigens such as CD10 and CD19.
CLL is a mature B-cell neoplasm, not a blast-based leukemia, and is not diagnosed by MPO.
Hairy cell leukemia is identified by TRAP positivity, not MPO.
exp: Myeloperoxidase (MPO) is a cytoplasmic enzyme specific to the granulocytic lineage, so MPO positivity in blasts confirms a myeloid origin and is a standard cytochemical stain (alongside flow cytometry) used to distinguish AML from ALL when blast morphology alone is ambiguous.

subject: Pathology
q: Crescents seen on light microscopy in rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis are composed predominantly of which cell type proliferating within Bowman's space?
opts: Proliferating parietal epithelial cells and infiltrating macrophages
why: Mesangial cell proliferation is the hallmark of mesangioproliferative diseases such as IgA nephropathy, not crescents.
Podocytes are effaced/injured in nephrotic syndromes but are not the main cellular component of a crescent.
Endothelial proliferation characterises diseases like diffuse proliferative lupus nephritis, not the crescent itself.
Correct — crescents are formed by proliferating parietal epithelial cells and infiltrating macrophages in Bowman's space.
exp: The glomerular crescent that defines rapidly progressive (crescentic) glomerulonephritis is formed by proliferating parietal epithelial cells of Bowman's capsule together with infiltrating macrophages, in response to severe capillary wall injury; extensive crescents (over half the glomeruli) predict rapid, severe loss of renal function regardless of the underlying cause — anti-GBM, immune-complex, or ANCA-associated.

subject: Pathology
q: Image described: a chest X-ray shows a centrally located, cavitating mass arising from a major bronchus in a long-term smoker, with associated hilar lymphadenopathy. Histology from bronchoscopic biopsy shows keratin pearls and intercellular bridges. Which lung cancer subtype is this?
why: Adenocarcinoma is typically peripheral and gland-forming/mucin-producing, not centrally cavitating with keratin pearls.
Small cell carcinoma is also central but shows small, blue, oat-shaped cells with neuroendocrine markers, not squamous differentiation.
Correct — central location, cavitation, keratin pearls and intercellular bridges are classic for squamous cell carcinoma.
Large cell carcinoma is an undifferentiated diagnosis of exclusion, lacking squamous or glandular features.
exp: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung is classically central, arising from bronchial epithelium via a smoking-driven metaplasia-dysplasia-carcinoma sequence, and is histologically defined by keratin pearls and intercellular bridges; it is also the classic cause of paraneoplastic hypercalcemia via PTHrP, unlike the now more common, peripherally located adenocarcinoma.

subject: Pathology
q: A medium-vessel vasculitis predominantly affecting children under 5 years, presenting with high fever for over 5 days, bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, strawberry tongue, polymorphous rash, and later periungual desquamation, carries its most serious risk from which complication?
why: RPGN is a feature of small-vessel, pauci-immune vasculitides such as GPA, not Kawasaki disease.
Correct — coronary artery vasculitis leading to aneurysm formation is the most feared complication of Kawasaki disease.
Mesenteric ischemia is a classic complication of polyarteritis nodosa, a different medium-vessel vasculitis.
Pulmonary hemorrhage is typical of anti-GBM disease or ANCA-associated vasculitis, not Kawasaki disease.
exp: Kawasaki disease is a medium-vessel vasculitis of early childhood, clinically diagnosed on fever for 5 days or more plus the classic mucocutaneous criteria; its most feared complication is coronary artery aneurysm, which is why IV immunoglobulin plus high-dose aspirin is started promptly, with echocardiographic follow-up to monitor the coronaries.

subject: Pathology
q: Serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), though non-specific, is most useful clinically as a marker of tumour burden and prognosis in which group of malignancies?
why: Correct — LDH is part of the standard staging/monitoring triad (with AFP and beta-hCG) in testicular germ cell tumours and is incorporated into lymphoma prognostic indices.
HCC is monitored with AFP, not LDH.
Cervical squamous cell carcinoma has no established LDH-based staging role.
RCC's paraneoplastic markers are ectopic EPO and PTHrP, not LDH.
exp: Serum LDH, though too non-specific to be diagnostic alone, is a validated marker of tumour burden and prognosis in germ cell tumours (part of the AFP/beta-hCG/LDH triad for testicular cancer staging) and in lymphomas, where it is one of the factors in the International Prognostic Index.

subject: Pathology
q: Image described: a child with an elfin (pixie-like) facies, mild intellectual disability, an unusually sociable/friendly personality, and echocardiography showing supravalvular aortic stenosis; hypercalcemia is noted on workup. Which genetic mechanism underlies this syndrome?
opts: Microdeletion of 7q11.23 involving the elastin gene
why: Trinucleotide repeat expansion causes disorders such as Fragile X syndrome or Huntington disease, not Williams syndrome.
Correct — a contiguous gene microdeletion at 7q11.23 including the elastin gene explains both the aortic/connective tissue findings and the facial/cognitive phenotype.
Maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 15 causes Prader-Willi syndrome, a different phenotype.
Robertsonian translocation is the mechanism in translocation Down syndrome, unrelated here.
exp: Williams syndrome results from a 7q11.23 microdeletion that includes the elastin (ELN) gene, whose haploinsufficiency explains the supravalvular aortic stenosis and connective-tissue findings, alongside the elfin facies, mild-moderate intellectual disability with a hypersociable personality, and infantile hypercalcemia; diagnosis is confirmed by FISH or microarray.

subject: Pathology
q: Image described: a peripheral blood smear from a patient with massive splenomegaly and long-standing marrow fibrosis shows teardrop-shaped red cells (dacrocytes) alongside immature myeloid and erythroid precursors ('leukoerythroblastic' picture). Which condition is most strongly suggested?
why: Iron deficiency anemia shows microcytic, hypochromic cells and pencil cells, not teardrop cells with a leukoerythroblastic picture.
Hereditary spherocytosis shows spherocytes with increased osmotic fragility, not teardrop cells.
Megaloblastic anemia shows macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils, not teardrop cells.
Correct — teardrop cells with a leukoerythroblastic smear and massive splenomegaly form the classic triad of primary myelofibrosis.
exp: Teardrop cells (dacrocytes) form when marrow fibrosis distorts red cells as they squeeze out of a fibrotic marrow space; combined with a leukoerythroblastic smear (circulating immature precursors from loss of the normal marrow-blood barrier) and massive splenomegaly from extramedullary hematopoiesis, this triad is classic for primary myelofibrosis.

subject: Pathology
q: Aschoff bodies (containing Anitschkow cells) found in the myocardium are pathognomonic of which condition?
why: Infective endocarditis shows vegetations of fibrin, platelets and organisms on valves, not Aschoff bodies.
Correct — Aschoff bodies containing Anitschkow cells are pathognomonic of acute rheumatic carditis.
Viral myocarditis shows lymphocytic infiltration with myocyte necrosis, not Aschoff bodies.
Kawasaki disease is a coronary artery vasculitis, not a cause of myocardial Aschoff bodies.
exp: Aschoff bodies are focal granulomatous myocardial lesions containing Anitschkow cells (macrophages with caterpillar-shaped nuclei) and multinucleated Aschoff giant cells, pathognomonic of acute rheumatic carditis — a delayed immune-mediated sequela of group A streptococcal pharyngitis via molecular mimicry — whose chronic scarring underlies rheumatic valve disease.
